cloze: After the argument, he sent a {{conciliatory}} note apologizing and proposing a compromise.
mnemonic: CONCILIATORY: CONCILE sounds like "reconcile".

definition: to reach a decision or opinion based on evidence; to end
examples: After reviewing the data, the researchers concluded that the drug was effective.
The author concludes the chapter with a summary of her main argument.
cloze: From the fossil evidence, scientists {{conclude}} that dinosaurs were warm-blooded.
mnemonic: CON-CLUDE: shut (close) the argument with a decision.

definition: to agree
examples: All three medical experts concurred that the painting was a clever forgery and not a genuine work.
The appeals judges concurred with the lower court's decision and rejected the company's lengthy objections.
cloze: I {{concur}} with your assessment that the plan needs more funding.
mnemonic: CON + CUR: running together in agreement.

definition: happening at the same time
examples: The study ran concurrent experiments in three different laboratories across Europe and North America.
Concurrent revolts in several provinces weakened the central government of the ancient empire.
cloze: Students may take two {{concurrent}} courses as long as the schedules do not overlap.
mnemonic: CON + CURRENT: running along together.

definition: to accept or overlook behavior regarded as wrong
examples: The school does not condone bullying in any form and punishes students who are caught engaging in it.
By saying nothing, he seemed to condone his friends' dishonest scheme, though he privately disapproved of it.
cloze: Few leaders would openly {{condone}} corruption among their own advisers.
mnemonic: CON + DONE: act as if the wrong is done and forgiven.

definition: to carry out or organize an activity
examples: Marine biologists conducted a survey of coral reefs along the northern coast.
The professor conducted an experiment to test how temperature affects plant growth.
cloze: Scientists plan to {{conduct}} further tests before publishing their findings.
mnemonic: CON-DUCT: lead (duct) an activity through.

definition: to keep within limits or restrict to a place
examples: Early experiments were confined to small laboratories because the equipment was bulky.
The disease was confined to a small area thanks to rapid quarantine measures.
cloze: The rules attempt to {{confine}} fishing to certain months of the year.
mnemonic: CON-FINE: keep it within a fine (limit) line.

definition: to establish that something is true
examples: Laboratory tests confirmed that the sample was far older than first believed.
The archaeologist's discovery confirmed the legend of the lost city.
cloze: Further experiments are needed to {{confirm}} the results.
mnemonic: CON-FIRM: make FIRM.

definition: a large, destructive fire
examples: A conflagration swept through the old harbor district and destroyed dozens of wooden warehouses.
The match dropped carelessly in the dry forest ignited a conflagration that burned for weeks.
cloze: The tiny spark grew into a {{conflagration}} that devoured the village within hours.
mnemonic: CON + FLAG: flames flagging across a field.

definition: to comply with rules, standards, or expectations
examples: All buildings in the district must conform to strict safety regulations.
Some scientists feared that young researchers would conform to prevailing theories rather than question them.
cloze: Students are expected to {{conform}} to the university's code of academic honesty.
mnemonic: CON-FORM: take the same form as others.

definition: to confuse or surprise; to prove wrong
examples: The sudden change in the rules confounded the beginners, who could no longer follow how the game worked.
The surprising results confounded the experts, whose careful predictions had turned out to be completely wrong.
cloze: The riddle will {{confound}} even clever students who think they know the answer.
mnemonic: CON-FOUND: found something that makes you perplexed.

definition: an expert judge in matters of taste or art
examples: As a wine connoisseur, he could identify a vintage with a single sip.
The gallery attracted connoisseurs willing to pay high prices for rare prints.
cloze: A true {{connoisseur}} of cheese, she could tell the region of origin from the aroma alone.
mnemonic: Connoisseur: "con-a-sewer" who knows fine things — sounds French "to know".

definition: following one after another without a break
examples: The region suffered three consecutive years of drought, devastating local farms.
The team won five consecutive championships between 2010 and 2015.
cloze: Students who miss two {{consecutive}} classes may be dropped from the course.
mnemonic: CONSECUTIVE: SEQUEL after SEQUEL in a row.

definition: as a result; therefore
examples: The soil was poor; consequently, the settlers struggled to grow enough food.
The dam failed, and consequently, the town downstream was flooded.
cloze: The library's funding was cut; {{consequently}}, it had to reduce its opening hours.
mnemonic: CONSEQUENCE + ly = as a result.

definition: fairly large in amount, size, or importance
examples: The new policy had a considerable impact on rural employment.
A considerable amount of ice has disappeared from the glacier in only two decades.
cloze: The expedition required {{considerable}} planning and a large amount of equipment.
mnemonic: CONSIDERable = worth considering because it is big.

definition: to be made up of; to have as the basic element
examples: The Earth's atmosphere consists mainly of nitrogen and oxygen, with traces of other gases.
The course consists of weekly lectures, small group discussions, and a final research project.
cloze: A healthy ecosystem will {{consist}} of many interdependent species.
mnemonic: CON-SIST: all parts sit (sist) together.

definition: clearly visible; attracting attention
examples: Wearing a bright red coat, she was conspicuous in the crowd.
He made a conspicuous effort to avoid looking at his former boss.
cloze: The ugly new tower is {{conspicuous}} against the old skyline of the city.
mnemonic: CON + SPICUOUS: spic = see; easily seen.

definition: anxiety or dismay caused by something unexpected
examples: News of the sudden resignation caused consternation among the staff.
To his consternation, the door was locked and his keys were inside.
cloze: The announcement filled the passengers with {{consternation}} as the plane lost altitude.
mnemonic: CONSTERNATION: your stomach turns over in a stern shock.

definition: to form or make up a whole; to be equal to
examples: Women constituted nearly half of the factory workforce by the end of the war.
Scientists debate what constitutes evidence of intelligent behavior in animals.
cloze: Leaves {{constitute}} the main part of the diet of these large herbivores.
mnemonic: CONSTITUTE: constitution = what a thing is made of.

definition: to limit or restrict someone or something
examples: Limited funds constrained the museum's ability to expand its collection.
Mountains constrained the early settlers to a narrow strip of fertile land.
cloze: Government regulations can {{constrain}} the growth of small businesses.
mnemonic: CON-STRAIN: strain tightly against freedom.

definition: belonging to the present time; living or happening at the same time
examples: The museum displays both ancient pottery and contemporary sculpture in its largest gallery.
Contemporary accounts of the plague describe the terror felt in the crowded medieval cities.
cloze: The author uses {{contemporary}} language to make the old story easier for modern readers.
mnemonic: CON-TEMPO-rary: with the same TEMPO of time.

definition: to assert; to compete or struggle
examples: Scientists contend that the climate is changing faster than earlier models had predicted, and urge immediate action.
Several strong teams will contend for the national championship this season, so the outcome is hard to predict.
cloze: The lawyer will {{contend}} that her client was not even in the city that night.
mnemonic: CONTEND: tend to fight with words.

definition: causing or likely to cause disagreement; argumentative
examples: The contentious debate over the new tax law divided the city council for the entire spring.
She avoided contentious topics like politics at family dinners to keep the peace among her relatives.
cloze: The {{contentious}} issue of water rights has divided the two regions for decades.
mnemonic: CONTENTious: a contest of tents? fights over everything.

definition: the circumstances or surrounding words that give meaning to something
examples: Readers can often guess a word's meaning from the context of the sentence.
Historians must understand the political context of a document before judging its message.
cloze: Taken out of {{context}}, the quote seems to say the opposite of what the speaker intended.
mnemonic: CON-TEXT: what goes with the text.

definition: to state the opposite of; to be inconsistent with
examples: The new evidence contradicts the earlier theory that the climate was stable.
Her findings contradicted those of previous studies, prompting further investigation.
cloze: Witnesses sometimes {{contradict}} one another when describing the same event.
mnemonic: CONTRA-DICT: speak (dict) against.

definition: a striking difference between two things
examples: The contrast between the dry plains and the green river valley was striking.
In contrast to earlier periods, the twentieth century saw rapid population growth.
cloze: The painter used a bold {{contrast}} of light and dark to create drama.
mnemonic: CONTRA-ST: stand against each other.

definition: to give something toward a common result; to help cause
examples: Volunteers contributed thousands of hours to restoring the wetland after the oil spill.
Deforestation contributes to soil erosion and the loss of habitats for many native animals.
cloze: Many factors may {{contribute}} to the success of a business startup.
mnemonic: CON-TRIBUTE: give a tribute together.

definition: feeling or showing remorse for wrongdoing
examples: The contrite thief wept openly in court and returned everything he had stolen from the shop.
She offered a contrite apology for forgetting her friend's birthday and promised to make up for it.
cloze: Looking {{contrite}}, the boy admitted he had broken the window.
mnemonic: CONTRITE: "con-trite" — you feel crushed (Latin terere, to rub).

definition: a prolonged public disagreement about something
examples: The dam project sparked controversy among environmentalists and local residents.
Scholars still debate the controversy over how the pyramids were built.
cloze: The new law has caused much {{controversy}} among teachers and parents.
mnemonic: CONTROVERSY: CONTRA + VERSE = verses against each other.

definition: stubbornly disobedient to authority
examples: The contumacious witness refused to answer the judge's questions and was held in contempt of court at once.
Contumacious students ignored every instruction from the dean and openly mocked the rules of the school.
cloze: The {{contumacious}} prisoner defied his guards at every turn.
mnemonic: Contumacious = contempt + tenacious: stubbornly contemptuous of authority.

definition: a confusing and difficult problem or puzzle
examples: The ethical conundrum left the committee deadlocked for weeks, since every option seemed equally unacceptable to someone.
How to cut costs without losing staff is a conundrum that troubles nearly every manager today.
cloze: The riddle was a real {{conundrum}}, and none of the students could solve it.
mnemonic: CONUNDRUM sounds like "can't understand rum".

definition: to come together for a meeting, or to call people to meet
examples: Delegates from forty nations convened in Geneva to discuss the climate agreement.
The dean convened a special committee to review the new curriculum.
cloze: The scientists will {{convene}} next month to share their latest research findings.
mnemonic: CON-VENE: come (ven) together.

definition: to change from one form or use to another
examples: Plants convert sunlight into chemical energy through the process known as photosynthesis.
The old factory was converted into an art museum that attracts thousands of visitors each year.
cloze: Engineers developed a machine that can {{convert}} ocean waves into electricity.
mnemonic: CON-VERT: turn (vert) into something else.

definition: extremely complex and difficult to follow
examples: The convoluted plot of the film confused even devoted fans.
He gave a convoluted explanation that only made things less clear.
cloze: The tax code's {{convoluted}} rules require an expert to understand them.
mnemonic: CON-VOLUTE: coiled, twisting like a spiral.

definition: to work together toward a shared goal
examples: Scientists from many nations cooperate to monitor the polar ice caps.
The two villages cooperated to build a dam that protected both from flooding.
cloze: Birds in the colony {{cooperate}} to defend their nests from predators.
mnemonic: CO-OPERATE: operate together.

definition: abundant; plentiful
examples: The student took copious notes during the lecture and filled three entire notebooks by the end of term.
Copious rainfall turned the dry, dusty valley bright green within just a few weeks of spring.
cloze: The chef used {{copious}} amounts of butter, so the sauce was extremely rich.
mnemonic: COPIOUS contains "copy" — lots of copies.

definition: warm, friendly, and polite
examples: The host gave us a cordial welcome and offered tea at once.
Relations between the neighboring countries remain cordial despite trade disputes.
cloze: Despite their rivalry, the two founders maintained a {{cordial}} relationship.
mnemonic: CORD = heart in Latin; a heartfelt greeting.

definition: to confirm or support with evidence
examples: Two eyewitnesses corroborated the defendant's account of where he had been on the night in question.
Later experiments corroborated the scientist's original hypothesis and silenced many of her early critics.
cloze: Fingerprints on the glass helped to {{corroborate}} the detective's suspicion that the suspect had been present.
mnemonic: CO + ROBORATE (robust): make a claim strong together.

definition: to tolerate or approve of
examples: The headmaster would not countenance cheating in any form and expelled students who were caught doing it.
The government could not countenance such flagrant abuse of power and quickly dismissed the officials involved.
cloze: We cannot {{countenance}} violence against peaceful protesters, whatever the reason.
mnemonic: COUNT + ENANCE: you "count" it as acceptable.

definition: to desire strongly something belonging to another
examples: She coveted her neighbor's beautiful garden and its blooming roses, and secretly wished that it were hers.
Many athletes covet the gold medal above all else and spend their whole lives training for it.
cloze: He secretly began to {{covet}} his friend's job and the status that came with it.
mnemonic: COVET: love it so, you "cover" it with your eyes.

definition: to crouch or shrink away in fear
examples: The frightened puppy cowered in the corner whenever anyone raised their voice.
Villagers cowered in their homes as the soldiers marched noisily through the streets.
cloze: Rather than {{cower}} before the bully, she stood tall and calmly demanded that he stop.
mnemonic: COWER sounds like "cow-er": a scared cow ducks.

definition: insensitive, tactless, and lacking refinement
examples: It was crass of him to brag about his bonus in front of laid-off colleagues.
Her crass jokes at the funeral shocked the mourners and offended the family.
cloze: The advertisement was {{crass}} in its use of a tragedy to sell expensive cars.
mnemonic: CRASS sounds like "grass" — rough, not manicured.

definition: contemptibly cowardly
examples: The craven soldier threw down his weapon and ran at the first shot.
Critics condemned the craven refusal of leaders to oppose injustice.
cloze: It was a {{craven}} act to blame an innocent colleague to avoid punishment.
mnemonic: CRAVEN sounds like "crave in" — hiding like a crow.

definition: too ready to believe things; gullible
examples: Credulous investors believed every promise the swindler made, and most lost their life savings to him.
The credulous child accepted her brother's tall tale about a talking dog living in the attic.
cloze: Only a {{credulous}} person would believe that a stranger wants to give away millions for free.
mnemonic: CRED = believe (credit); credulous believes too much.

definition: extremely important, or involving careful judgment
examples: Critical thinking allows students to question assumptions and evaluate evidence.
Water is critical to survival in the harsh desert environment.
cloze: The hospital faced a {{critical}} shortage of blood donors.
mnemonic: CRITICAL = CRITIC judges carefully.

definition: extremely important; decisive
examples: Water is crucial to the survival of every living organism.
Her crucial discovery transformed the way scientists understand the immune system.
cloze: Accurate measurements are {{crucial}} in any scientific experiment.
mnemonic: CRUCIAL = CRUX (the central point).

definition: the decisive or most important point
examples: The crux of the problem is that the funding is simply inadequate.
She went straight to the crux of the matter in her opening statement.
cloze: The {{crux}} of the dispute is who actually owns the land.
mnemonic: CRUX is like cross — the crossing point.

definition: having a hidden or puzzling meaning
examples: She left behind a cryptic message that nobody in the family was able to decipher.
The detective puzzled for hours over the cryptic clue scrawled on the wall in red chalk.
cloze: His {{cryptic}} reply left everyone wondering what he actually meant.
mnemonic: CRYPT: a hidden, dark chamber with secrets.

definition: to select from a large group; to remove unfit members
examples: The editor culled the best stories from hundreds of submissions to create a short, strong anthology.
Farmers were forced to cull the infected herd in order to stop the disease from spreading further.
cloze: The researcher spent months trying to {{cull}} reliable data from hundreds of old records.
mnemonic: CULL sounds like "pull" — pull out the best.

definition: to reach a final or highest point
examples: Years of grueling training culminated in her winning the gold medal at the national championships.
The tense negotiations, which dragged on for months, culminated in a historic peace agreement between the two nations.
cloze: The festival will {{culminate}} in a spectacular fireworks show on the final night.
mnemonic: CULMEN = top; reach the peak.

definition: deserving blame for wrongdoing
examples: The inquiry found the captain culpable for ignoring the storm warnings.
She felt culpable for the accident, though she had not caused it directly.
cloze: The court held the manufacturer {{culpable}} in the deaths because it knew of the fault.
mnemonic: CULPABLE contains "culprit" — the guilty one.

definition: clumsy and awkward to carry or use
examples: The cumbersome old computer took up half the desk and made a terrible noise whenever it started.
The cumbersome approval process, requiring seven signatures, delayed the project by several months and frustrated everyone involved.
cloze: Carrying the {{cumbersome}} suitcase up three flights of stairs exhausted her.
mnemonic: CUMBER-some: it burdens you with some weight.

definition: increasing gradually by successive additions
examples: The cumulative effect of small changes in temperature can alter an entire ecosystem.
Learning is cumulative: new knowledge builds on what students already understand.
cloze: The {{cumulative}} rainfall over the season was higher than in any previous year.
mnemonic: CUMULATIVE: CUMULUS clouds pile up.

definition: extreme greed, especially for money
examples: The cupidity of the landlords drove rents beyond what families could pay.
Their cupidity was aroused by rumors of gold in the hills.
cloze: His {{cupidity}} was obvious as he eyed the open safe filled with jewels.
mnemonic: CUPID wants things — wanting wealth, not love.

definition: to restrict or keep within limits
examples: Governments introduced taxes to curb the use of fossil fuels.
The treatment helped curb the spread of the infection through the village.
cloze: Strict measures were taken to {{curb}} illegal fishing in the protected waters.
mnemonic: CURB the dog like a curb holds the road edge.

definition: a bad-tempered, difficult person, often old
examples: The curmudgeon next door complained whenever children played in the street, whatever the time of day.
Beneath the grumpy exterior of the old curmudgeon lay a surprisingly warm heart and a dry sense of humor.
cloze: The {{curmudgeon}} grumbled about the noise, the weather, and the price of bread.
mnemonic: CURMUDGEON: a "cur" (mean dog) and "mudgeon" mud-grumpy.

definition: hasty and superficial; done without attention to detail
examples: He gave the long contract only a cursory glance before signing it, and later regretted his haste.
A cursory inspection of the wall missed the deep crack hidden behind the old wallpaper.
cloze: After a {{cursory}} review of the report, she realized she had overlooked several errors.
mnemonic: CURSORY: cursor racing over the page quickly.

definition: to reduce or cut short
examples: The company curtailed overtime hours across all departments in an effort to save money this year.
Heavy snow forced the airline to curtail its flights and strand thousands of travelers overnight.
cloze: Budget cuts will {{curtail}} the library's opening hours starting next month.
mnemonic: CURT + TAIL: cut the tail short.

definition: according to the usual habit or tradition
examples: It is customary in many cultures to remove shoes before entering a home.
Customary law, passed down orally, governed the village for centuries.
cloze: In academic writing, it is {{customary}} to cite previous research on the topic.
mnemonic: CUSTOMary = following CUSTOM.

definition: distrustful of people's motives; believing selfishness drives all
examples: The cynical reporter assumed every politician was lying for personal gain.
Her cynical remark that charity is just show offended the organizers.
cloze: He grew {{cynical}} about public service after seeing how many officials accepted bribes.
mnemonic: CYNIC: sounds like "sin-ic" — sees sin everywhere.

definition: a scarcity or lack of something
examples: A dearth of rainfall left the reservoirs nearly empty by August.
The town suffered a dearth of skilled nurses after the hospital cut salaries.
cloze: Because of a {{dearth}} of reliable data, the economists hesitated to publish any forecast.
mnemonic: DEARth sounds like DEAR: when something is dear (costly), there is little of it.

definition: a sudden, humiliating failure or collapse
examples: The merger turned into a debacle that cost the firm millions and its reputation.
After the election debacle, the party's leaders resigned in disgrace.
cloze: The product launch was a complete {{debacle}}: the website crashed, shipments were lost, and customers demanded refunds.
mnemonic: DEBACLE: the dam BREAKS (French débâcle, a breaking up of ice) and everything collapses.

definition: to lower the quality, value, or dignity of something
examples: Critics said that constant advertising debased the once-noble tradition of the festival.
Rulers who debased the coinage mixed cheap metal into silver to fund their wars.
cloze: Politicians who lie so openly {{debase}} public discourse for everyone.
mnemonic: DE-BASE: send something down to the base, the bottom.

definition: to weaken seriously; to sap the strength of
examples: The long illness debilitated him so badly that he could barely climb the stairs without help.
Years of drought debilitated the region's farming economy and forced many families to leave.
cloze: A {{debilitating}} fever kept the explorer in bed for weeks and drained all his strength.
mnemonic: DEBILITate contains ABILITY with a 'de-' prefix: it removes your ability.

definition: to become smaller, weaker, or less; to refuse politely
examples: Populations of some amphibians have declined sharply over the past thirty years.
Trade along the old caravan route declined once ships began carrying goods by sea.
cloze: If funding continues to {{decline}}, the research station may have to close.
mnemonic: DE-CLINE: slope (cline) downward.

definition: polite, dignified behavior that fits a formal occasion
examples: Even in the heated debate, the senator maintained perfect decorum.
The students were reminded that courtroom decorum forbids talking or eating during the trial.
cloze: The children's loud shouting at the funeral offended mourners who expected quiet {{decorum}}.
mnemonic: DECORum: DECORated manners, neat and proper like a decorated room.

definition: to reach a conclusion by reasoning from evidence
examples: From the layers of rock, geologists deduced the sequence of ancient volcanic eruptions.
Detectives deduce the identity of a thief from small clues left at the scene.
cloze: Scientists can {{deduce}} the age of a tree by counting the rings in its trunk.
mnemonic: DE-DUCE: lead (duce) down from evidence.

definition: respectful submission to another's judgment or wishes
examples: The young lawyer spoke with deference to the veteran judge.
Out of deference to her grandfather's age, they let him choose the restaurant.
cloze: In {{deference}} to the host's customs, the guests removed their shoes at the door.
mnemonic: DEFER to someone: you put their wishes first.

definition: to state the exact meaning of, or to outline clearly
examples: Linguists define a dialect as a regional variety of a language.
The treaty defined the border between the two countries along the river.
cloze: Teachers often ask students to {{define}} new terms in their own words.
mnemonic: DE-FINE: set the FINE edges (fin = end) of a meaning.

definition: harmful, especially in a way that is not obvious
examples: Prolonged exposure to the chemical has a deleterious effect on the liver.
Critics argued that the new policy would have deleterious consequences for small farmers.
cloze: Smoking is {{deleterious}} to health, yet its damage often appears only after decades.
mnemonic: DELETE-rious: it deletes your health.

definition: done on purpose and after careful thought
examples: The government made a deliberate choice to invest in public transportation.
The scientist's slow and deliberate movements prevented her from scaring the birds.
cloze: The destruction of the monument was a {{deliberate}} act, not an accident.
mnemonic: DE-LIBERATE: weigh like a LIBRA (scale).

definition: to describe or outline something precisely
examples: The report delineates the responsibilities of each department in careful detail.
Surveyors delineated the boundary between the two estates with stakes and flags.
cloze: The lawyer tried to {{delineate}} exactly where the company's liability began and ended.
mnemonic: DE-LINE-ate: draw the LINES that show the shape.

definition: to show clearly by giving proof or evidence
examples: The experiment demonstrated that plants grow faster with extra light.
The teacher demonstrated the procedure before asking students to try it.
cloze: Her results {{demonstrate}} a clear link between sleep and academic performance.
mnemonic: DEMON-STRATE: show it like a demo.

definition: to criticize unfairly; to belittle someone's reputation
examples: Rivals sought to denigrate her achievements by calling them mere luck.
He never denigrated his opponents, preferring to argue against their ideas instead.
cloze: Rather than answering the charges, the candidate chose to {{denigrate}} his accuser's character.
mnemonic: DE-NIGRA-te: in Latin 'nigrare' means to blacken; you blacken someone's name.

definition: to publicly condemn as wrong or evil
examples: Leaders publicly denounced the attack as cowardly and barbaric, and demanded that the culprits be punished.
The newspaper denounced the corrupt officials in a fiery editorial that called for their immediate resignation.
cloze: Human rights groups were quick to {{denounce}} the regime's treatment of prisoners.
mnemonic: DE-NOUNCE: announce (nuntiare) against someone.

definition: closely packed together; thick
examples: The dense forest blocked sunlight from reaching the ground, so few plants grew below.
The most densely populated regions of the world are found in South and East Asia.
cloze: A {{dense}} fog covered the harbor, making it hard to see the ships.
mnemonic: DENSE sounds like THICK: DENSE = tightly packed.

definition: to use up or reduce greatly
examples: Overfishing for decades has depleted the ocean's fish stocks, and many species are now nearly gone.
The long trek through the mountains depleted the hikers' supplies of food and water within a week.
cloze: Constant farming can {{deplete}} the soil of vital nutrients.
mnemonic: DE-PLETE: opposite of COMPLETE; empty it.

definition: to feel or express strong disapproval of
examples: The mayor deplored the vandalism of the memorial, calling it a shameful insult to the city's history.
Many teachers deplore the decline of reading among teenagers, who now prefer short videos to books.
cloze: Critics {{deplore}} the use of violence, no matter what the cause.
mnemonic: DE-PLORE: weep (plorare) over something awful.

definition: to express disapproval of; to belittle
examples: She deprecated her own talent, insisting in every interview that she was merely lucky and not gifted.
Teachers deprecated the use of calculators in the early grades, warning that students would never learn arithmetic.
cloze: The scientist tended to {{deprecate}} his own accomplishments, calling them minor.
mnemonic: DE-PRECATE: pray (precari) that something goes AWAY.

definition: to mock or ridicule contemptuously
examples: Classmates derided his old-fashioned clothes and laughed behind his back until he finally stopped wearing them.
Early critics derided the invention as a useless toy that nobody would ever want to buy.
cloze: The crowd began to {{deride}} the speaker, jeering and laughing at every mistake.
mnemonic: DERIDE: a RIDE on someone's feelings, laughing as you go (also 'risus', laughter).

definition: contemptuous ridicule
examples: The mayor's proposal was greeted with derision from the council.
Early inventors often faced derision from those who could not imagine the future.
cloze: His suggestion was met with {{derision}}; people laughed openly at the idea.
mnemonic: Noun of DERIDE: laughter at someone.

definition: imitating the work of others; not original
examples: Reviewers dismissed the novel as derivative, a patchwork of better earlier books.
Her early paintings were derivative, echoing the style of her famous teacher.
cloze: The band's new album sounds {{derivative}}, as if it borrowed every riff from older groups.
mnemonic: DERIVE: the idea is derived from elsewhere, not new.

definition: to obtain or come from a source
examples: Many English words are derived from Latin and Greek roots.
Early societies derived most of their food from hunting and gathering.
cloze: The ancient city's wealth was {{derived}} mainly from trade along the silk routes.
mnemonic: DERIVE: from the RIVER (rive): comes downstream from a source.

definition: to dry out completely; to remove moisture
examples: The desert wind desiccated the soil until it cracked like old leather.
Fruit is often desiccated so it can be stored for months.
cloze: The explorers found a {{desiccated}} riverbed, hard and cracked, where water had once flowed.
mnemonic: DESERT + SICCATE (dry): a desert desiccates.

definition: to officially name or set aside for a purpose
examples: The government designated the forest as a protected national park.
The committee designated one member to present its findings to the board.
cloze: The area was {{designated}} as a site of special scientific interest.
mnemonic: DESIGNATE: put a SIGN on it.

definition: a ruler with absolute power, often cruel
examples: The despot ruled by fear, jailing anyone who criticized him.
Citizens finally rose up against the despot who had stolen their freedoms.
cloze: The {{despot}} crushed all opposition and ruled without laws for thirty years.
mnemonic: DESPOT: a DEPOT of power in one man's hands.

definition: lacking basic necessities; extremely poor
examples: The flood left thousands of families destitute and homeless, without clothes, food, or any money at all.
He died destitute, having spent his entire fortune on gambling, bad investments, and expensive parties.
cloze: The charity helps {{destitute}} families who lack even food and shelter.
mnemonic: DE-STITUTE: STATIONED (put) down at the bottom with nothing.

definition: lacking a plan or enthusiasm; jumping randomly from one thing to another
examples: The two men made desultory conversation, drifting from weather to sports to nothing.
After losing interest, he made only a desultory effort to finish the project.
cloze: The audience gave only {{desultory}} applause, clearly bored by the lecture.
mnemonic: Latin 'desultor' was a circus rider who leaped from horse to horse, hopping around.

definition: to discover or notice something that is hard to see
examples: Satellites can detect small changes in the height of the ocean surface.
Doctors detected the disease early, which greatly improved the patient's chances of recovery.
cloze: Special sensors in the lake can {{detect}} even tiny traces of pollution.
mnemonic: DETECT: a DETECTive finds clues.

definition: to discourage someone from acting by fear or difficulty
examples: High fences and security cameras are meant to deter thieves from even attempting to break into the warehouse.
Neither the freezing cold nor the long queue deterred the loyal fans from waiting outside overnight.
cloze: Harsh penalties are intended to {{deter}} people from committing crimes in the first place.
mnemonic: DETER sounds like 'deterrent': a DOOR-er that turns you away.

definition: to become progressively worse
examples: The paintings began to deteriorate after years of exposure to moisture and light.
As pollution increased, the quality of the river water steadily deteriorated.
cloze: Without regular maintenance, the old stone bridge will {{deteriorate}} rapidly.
mnemonic: DE-TERIOR: becoming more 'inferior'.

definition: causing harm or damage
examples: Lack of sleep over a long period is detrimental to your health, memory, and general mood.
The scandal had a detrimental effect on the company's reputation, and sales fell sharply within months.
cloze: Excessive noise can be {{detrimental}} to children's learning and concentration.
mnemonic: DETRIMENTAL: a DETriMENT, a damage.

definition: to depart from a standard or usual course
examples: The comet deviates from its predicted path because of the gravity of nearby planets.
Few artists of the period deviated from the strict rules of classical painting.
cloze: Researchers must not {{deviate}} from the approved procedure during the experiment.
mnemonic: DE-VIATE: leave the VIA (road).

definition: to give time, effort, or resources to a particular purpose
examples: She devoted her career to studying the migration patterns of whales.
The city devoted a large part of its budget to public transport.
cloze: Many students {{devote}} several hours each day to preparing for the exam.
mnemonic: DE-VOTE: give your VOTE (vow) to it.

definition: a bitter, lengthy verbal attack
examples: The coach launched into a diatribe against the referees that lasted ten minutes.
Her editorial was less an argument than a diatribe against modern life.
cloze: Instead of a calm discussion, the meeting turned into a {{diatribe}} against the manager.
mnemonic: DIA-TRIBE: a DIRE TRIBE shouting at you.

definition: a division into two sharply opposed parts or ideas
examples: There is a dichotomy between the city's glittering center and its poor outskirts.
The essay challenges the supposed dichotomy between art and science.
cloze: The {{dichotomy}} between what the leader says in public and does in private shocked voters.
mnemonic: DI = two, CHOTOMY = cut: cut in two.

definition: intended to teach, often in an overly moralizing way
examples: The film was so didactic that it felt like a lecture on honesty.
Fables are didactic stories that end with a clear moral lesson.
cloze: Readers found the novel too {{didactic}}, since every chapter preached a lesson about thrift.
mnemonic: DIDACTic: a DICTATOR who teaches you with a stick.

definition: shy and lacking self-confidence
examples: The diffident student rarely raised his hand in class, even though he usually knew every answer.
Her diffident, hesitant manner hid considerable talent, and few colleagues suspected how capable she really was.
cloze: Too {{diffident}} to introduce himself, he stood alone at the edge of the party.
mnemonic: DIFFIDENT: DIFFerent from the crowd, afraid to speak up (no FIDence, i.e. confidence).

definition: to wander away from the main topic in speaking or writing
examples: The professor often digressed into long stories about his childhood, and the lecture never reached its point.
If I may digress for a moment, I want to mention an earlier experiment that surprised us.
cloze: Please don't {{digress}}; we have only ten minutes left and must reach the main point.
mnemonic: DI-GRESS: go (gress) away from the path.

definition: slow to act; tending to delay
examples: The dilatory clerk let the paperwork sit on his desk for weeks.
Critics accused the government of being dilatory in responding to the flood.
cloze: His {{dilatory}} habits, always putting tasks off until the last minute, cost him the promotion.
mnemonic: DILATORY sounds like DELAY.

definition: a person who dabbles in a field without serious commitment
examples: The wealthy dilettante dabbled in painting, music, and poetry but mastered none.
Experts scorned him as a mere dilettante who read a few books and claimed expertise.
cloze: Unlike the professional historians, he was a {{dilettante}} who studied the past only as a hobby.
mnemonic: DILETTANTE: DILLY-DALLY with many hobbies.

definition: to become or make smaller or less
examples: The glacier's size has diminished dramatically over the past century.
Constant noise can diminish a person's ability to concentrate on difficult tasks.
cloze: As sources of food {{diminish}}, animal populations will begin to shrink.
mnemonic: DIMinish: lights DIM and get smaller.

definition: extremely small
examples: The diminutive frog is hardly larger than a coin, yet its poison is deadly.
Despite his diminutive size, the explorer survived the harsh expedition better than most.
cloze: The island is home to a {{diminutive}} species of deer found nowhere else.
mnemonic: DIMINUTIVE: DIMINish to tiny.

definition: to free someone from a false belief
examples: I hated to disabuse her of the notion that the job would be easy.
The experiment disabused scientists of the idea that the particle was stable.
cloze: It took years of failure to {{disabuse}} him of the illusion that success comes without effort.
mnemonic: DIS-ABUSE: remove the abuse of a false idea.

definition: to perceive or recognize something that is not obvious
examples: It was hard to discern any pattern in the scattered data.
In the dim light, she could just discern a figure at the end of the street.
cloze: A good editor can {{discern}} the strong ideas hidden inside a messy draft.
mnemonic: DIS-CERN: sift apart (like a sieve) to see differences.

definition: to unsettle or make uneasy
examples: His sudden, unexpected silence disconcerted the interviewers, who had expected a confident and talkative candidate.
The strange question disconcerted her so badly that she lost her train of thought and blushed.
cloze: Her blunt question seemed to {{disconcert}} the speaker, who stammered for a reply.
mnemonic: DIS-CONCERT: breaks the CONCERT, throws you out of harmony.

definition: clashing or not in harmony
examples: The orchestra's discordant notes clashed so badly that the whole audience winced in their seats.
The committee's discordant opinions, with no two members agreeing, made a decision seem almost impossible.
cloze: Her calm manner was {{discordant}} with the panic all around her.
mnemonic: DIS-CORD: the chords do not agree.

definition: to harm the reputation of; to make seem false
examples: The scandal discredited the senator and quickly ended his long career in national politics.
New evidence discredited the key witness's testimony, and the jury no longer believed anything he had said.
cloze: Rivals tried to {{discredit}} the researcher by questioning her data.
mnemonic: DIS-CREDIT: remove credit.

definition: a difference between things that should match
examples: Auditors found a discrepancy between the sales figures and the bank deposits.
The discrepancy in the two witnesses' accounts puzzled the detective.
cloze: A glaring {{discrepancy}} between his story and the video footage raised suspicion.
mnemonic: DIS-CREPANCY: things do not CREEP along together.

definition: careful judgment in speech or action; freedom to decide
examples: A diplomat must use discretion when speaking to the press.
The manager has the discretion to grant extra time to employees who need it.
cloze: The doctor's {{discretion}} ensured that no patient's secrets ever leaked.
mnemonic: DIS-CRETION: from 'discern', knowing how to separate wise from unwise words.

definition: rambling from one topic to another
examples: The professor's discursive lectures wandered across history, art, and politics, and students rarely knew what the main topic was.
Her discursive essay lacked a clear thesis, drifting from one interesting tangent to the next without a conclusion.
cloze: The speech was long and {{discursive}}, jumping from one topic to the next without a point.
mnemonic: DISCURSIVE: DISCOURSE that runs here and there.

definition: contempt for something seen as unworthy
examples: She looked at the cheap souvenirs on the table with open disdain and refused even to touch them.
His deep disdain for authority, shown by constant mockery of his teachers, got him into trouble at school.
cloze: The critic's {{disdain}} for popular fiction was clear in every review.
mnemonic: DIS-DAIN: do not DEIGN to notice it.

definition: not candid; pretending to be naive or sincere
examples: It was disingenuous of him to claim he had not known about the problem, when he had written the memo himself.
The company's disingenuous apology, full of false regret, fooled no one who had read the leaked emails.
cloze: Her {{disingenuous}} surprise at the news fooled no one, since she had planned it herself.
mnemonic: DIS-INGENUOUS: not genuine, not frank.

definition: impartial; not influenced by personal gain
examples: A disinterested referee must have no stake in either team.
The court sought a disinterested expert to evaluate the evidence.
cloze: We need a {{disinterested}} judge with no financial stake in the outcome.
mnemonic: DIS-INTERESTED: you have no interest (stake) in the result. Not the same as bored.

definition: to speak of someone or something as unimportant or poor
examples: Rivals disparaged her research as superficial, without reading it closely.
He never disparaged his colleagues, even when he disagreed with them.
cloze: It is unkind to {{disparage}} a friend's efforts when she has worked so hard.
mnemonic: DIS-PARAGE: remove the PARity (equal status) of someone.

definition: fundamentally different; unable to be compared
examples: The two sisters have disparate tastes in music and food.
The committee had to unite disparate groups with little in common.
cloze: Scholars from {{disparate}} fields, from physics to poetry, gathered at the conference.
mnemonic: DISPARATE: DIS-PAIR-ate: they will never be a pair.

definition: not influenced by strong emotion; impartial
examples: A judge must give a dispassionate reading of the facts.
She gave a dispassionate account of the accident, without anger or blame.
cloze: His {{dispassionate}} analysis of the crisis ignored how upset the victims felt.
mnemonic: DIS-PASSION: without passion.

definition: to spread widely or scatter in different directions
examples: Wind helps disperse the seeds of many plants over long distances.
The crowd dispersed quickly when the storm clouds rolled over the stadium.
cloze: Birds help to {{disperse}} seeds across the forest by carrying fruit.
mnemonic: DIS-PERSE: persons flying apart.

definition: a disagreement or argument, especially over a formal matter
examples: A long dispute over land rights divided the two neighboring communities.
The dispute between the scientists centered on how the data should be interpreted.
cloze: The two nations settled their {{dispute}} through peaceful negotiation.
mnemonic: DIS-PUTE: put two sides apart.

definition: to hide one's true feelings or intentions behind a false appearance
examples: He dissembled his fury behind a pleasant smile, so that nobody in the room guessed how angry he was.
Politicians sometimes dissemble, pretending to agree with everyone, to avoid giving a clear answer to a hard question.
cloze: Unable to {{dissemble}} any longer, she finally told them what she truly felt.
mnemonic: DIS-SEMBLE: you make yourself RESEMBLE something you are not.

definition: to spread widely, especially information
examples: The Internet allows news to be disseminated to millions of readers within a few seconds of an event.
Volunteers disseminated pamphlets about the new vaccine across the region, going door to door in every village.
cloze: The organization works to {{disseminate}} scientific findings to the general public.
mnemonic: DIS-SEMEN-ate: scatter seeds (Latin semen) in all directions.

definition: a clash of sounds or ideas that do not fit together
examples: The composer used dissonance to create a feeling of tension.
The dissonance between her words and her expression was obvious.
cloze: Cognitive {{dissonance}} arises when a person's beliefs conflict with his actions.
mnemonic: DIS-SONANCE: bad SOUND together.

definition: to persuade someone not to do something
examples: We tried to dissuade him from quitting, but his mind was made up.
Heavy rain failed to dissuade the crowd from attending the parade.
cloze: Her parents tried to {{dissuade}} her from sailing alone across the ocean.
mnemonic: DIS-SUADE: un-persuade; SUAVE talk away from a plan.

definition: clearly different or separate; easily noticed
examples: The two species look alike but have distinct songs that scientists can tell apart.
Each region of the country has its own distinct cuisine and traditions.
cloze: The city's old and new districts are quite {{distinct}} in architecture.
mnemonic: DISTINCT: stands apart, like a dis-TINCT color.

definition: to twist or change the true shape, meaning, or sound
examples: The curved glass distorted the image of the building on the lake.
Critics claimed that the report distorted the facts to support a political agenda.
cloze: Heat above the road can {{distort}} the light and create the illusion of water.
mnemonic: DIS-TORT: a tort (twist) away from truth.

definition: to give out or spread among many
examples: The government distributed seeds to farmers affected by the drought.
Wind and animals distribute seeds across wide areas of grassland.
cloze: Volunteers will {{distribute}} food to families who lost their homes.
mnemonic: DIS-TRIBUTE: give tribute out to each.

definition: to separate and go in different directions
examples: The two paths diverge at the old oak tree, so hikers must choose between the left and right.
Their opinions diverged sharply once they began discussing money, and the friendly talk quickly became an argument.
cloze: The roads {{diverge}} a mile ahead, one heading north and the other west.
mnemonic: DI-VERGE: the road is at the VERGE of splitting into two.

definition: showing a great deal of variety; very different
examples: The rainforest is home to an extraordinarily diverse range of plant and insect species.
The university attracts students from diverse cultural and educational backgrounds.
cloze: The region's {{diverse}} economy includes farming, tourism, and technology.
mnemonic: DI-VERSE: many VERSEs, many versions.

definition: to reveal private or secret information
examples: The spy refused to divulge the names of his contacts.
Doctors may not divulge a patient's medical details without permission.
cloze: She promised not to {{divulge}} the secret, even if pressed by her closest friends.
mnemonic: DIVULGE: DIVE and let the VULGAR public know it.

definition: easily taught or led; submissive
examples: The docile horse followed its trainer across the field without any fuss, as if it were tame as a dog.
A docile workforce rarely questions management's decisions, even when those decisions seem unfair or unwise to outsiders.
cloze: The normally {{docile}} child suddenly refused to follow instructions.
mnemonic: DOCILE comes from Latin docere, 'to teach': easy to teach.

definition: rigidly applying a theory regardless of practicality
examples: His doctrinaire approach ignored the practical needs of the workers, because he cared more about theory than results.
The party's doctrinaire leaders rejected any compromise and insisted that every rule be followed exactly as written.
cloze: The {{doctrinaire}} minister refused to adapt his theory even when it clearly failed.
mnemonic: DOCTRINE-aire: a person who sticks to doctrine at all costs.

definition: stubbornly asserting opinions as undeniable truth
examples: His dogmatic insistence that he alone was right ended every discussion.
The scientist warned against being dogmatic about theories that lack proof.
cloze: A {{dogmatic}} leader, he refused to consider any views other than his own.
mnemonic: DOG-matic: a DOG that barks one thing and never listens.

definition: a specific area of knowledge, activity, or control
examples: Marine biology is a domain that combines chemistry, ecology, and geology.
Until recently, space exploration was the exclusive domain of national governments.
cloze: The study of language falls within the {{domain}} of linguistics and psychology.
mnemonic: DOMAIN = DOMinion's area.

definition: relating to the home or to one's own country
examples: Dogs were among the first domestic animals, bred from wolves thousands of years ago.
Domestic manufacturing declined as cheaper imports entered the market and consumers changed their habits.
cloze: The economy grew because of strong {{domestic}} demand rather than exports.
mnemonic: DOMESTIC: DOMicile (home).

definition: most important, powerful, or noticeable
examples: Lions are the dominant predators in the African savanna, hunting zebras and antelope.
Latin remained the dominant language of European scholarship for many centuries after the empire fell.
cloze: The {{dominant}} male in the group usually has first access to food.
mnemonic: DOMINANT: DOMINATES the others.

definition: temporarily inactive, as if asleep
examples: The volcano has been dormant for centuries but could erupt again.
Many seeds lie dormant in the soil until spring rain arrives.
cloze: Her talent for painting remained {{dormant}} until she retired and finally had the time.
mnemonic: DORMant: like a DORMitory at night, quiet and asleep.

definition: stern, gloomy, and unfriendly in manner
examples: The dour old man glared sternly at the children playing in the street outside his gloomy house.
Her dour expression and tight lips suggested at once that the news from the doctor was very bad.
cloze: Despite the festive mood, the {{dour}} host scowled all evening.
mnemonic: DOUR rhymes with SOUR: a sour face.

definition: extreme in effect; severe and sudden
examples: Drastic changes in temperature killed much of the coral in the bay.
The company took drastic measures to reduce costs after profits fell sharply.
cloze: The government adopted {{drastic}} steps to prevent the economy from collapsing.
mnemonic: DRASTIC sounds like DRAMATIC and plastic: big change.

definition: amusing in an odd, understated way
examples: He had a droll sense of humor that made even meetings enjoyable.
The comedian's droll remarks delighted the audience without a single raised voice.
cloze: Her {{droll}} observations about office life made colleagues smile quietly.
mnemonic: DROLL sounds like TROLL: an odd little creature that makes you chuckle.

definition: doubtful; of questionable value or honesty
examples: The claim seemed dubious to most scientists, since no experiment had ever produced evidence to support it.
He made his fortune by dubious means that investigators later examined with great suspicion.
cloze: I am {{dubious}} about the plan, because it assumes everything will go perfectly.
mnemonic: DUBious sounds like DOUBT.

definition: to deceive or trick
examples: Con artists duped the retirees out of their life savings by promising huge profits that never existed.
He felt foolish after being duped by a fake email that pretended to come from his bank.
cloze: Scammers tried to {{dupe}} elderly customers into paying for a worthless product.
mnemonic: A DUPE falls for a trick like a fool who 'DOOPS' himself.

definition: deceitful double-dealing; speaking or acting two ways
examples: The diplomat's duplicity came to light when both sides compared his promises.
He was shocked by her duplicity, since she had praised him publicly while undermining him in private.
cloze: The spy's {{duplicity}} was exposed when both countries discovered he was working for each side.
mnemonic: DUPLI-city: DUPLICATE faces, two-faced.

definition: to gradually become smaller or fewer
examples: The number of wild tigers has dwindled to only a few thousand.
As funding dwindled, the research team had to abandon several projects.
cloze: Supplies of fresh water will {{dwindle}} if the rains fail again.
mnemonic: DWINDLE: small like a WINDLE of candle, getting thin.

definition: to flow back or gradually weaken
examples: As the tide ebbed, the fishing boats were left resting on the wet sand far from the water.
Her enthusiasm for the project slowly ebbed as the work dragged on month after tiresome month.
cloze: As support for the strike began to {{ebb}}, more workers returned to their jobs.
mnemonic: EBB sounds like a falling tide.

definition: overflowing with enthusiasm and high spirits
examples: The ebullient coach hugged every player after the win, laughing and shouting with uncontainable joy.
Her ebullient personality, bubbling with enthusiasm and humor, made her the soul of every party she attended.
cloze: The team was {{ebullient}} after the victory, singing and dancing in the locker room.
mnemonic: EBULLIENT: like water that BOILS over (Latin bullire) with joy.

definition: drawing from many different sources or styles
examples: Her eclectic taste in music ranges from opera to punk rock.
The museum's eclectic collection includes Roman coins and modern posters.
cloze: He has {{eclectic}} interests, from medieval history to ocean biology.
mnemonic: E-CLECTIC: you select (Greek eklegein) from everything.

definition: to erase or make inconspicuous
examples: Time and weather had effaced the inscription on the old tombstone until no letter could be read.
Shy and nervous, he tried to efface himself and stay out of the loud argument at the table.
cloze: Centuries of wind and rain had begun to {{efface}} the carvings on the monument.
mnemonic: EF-FACE: rub out the FACE of an image.

definition: bubbly and lively; giving off bubbles
examples: The effervescent hostess welcomed everyone at the door with a warm laugh and a lively word.
Soda is effervescent because dissolved carbon dioxide escapes in tiny bubbles whenever the bottle is opened.
cloze: Her {{effervescent}} personality lifted the mood of every room she entered.
mnemonic: EFFERVESCENT: like an EFFERVESCENT antacid, FIZZING.

definition: weak, overrefined, and lacking vigor
examples: The novel mocks the effete aristocrats who had grown too soft for life.
Critics dismissed the committee as an effete group out of touch with real work.
cloze: The once-vigorous empire had become {{effete}}, dependent on mercenaries for its defense.
mnemonic: EFFETE: worn out like an exhausted hen that has laid all its eggs.

definition: the power to produce a desired result
examples: Trials confirmed the efficacy of the new drug against the virus.
Some doubt the efficacy of sanctions in changing a country's policy.
cloze: Doctors tested the {{efficacy}} of the vaccine on thousands of volunteers.
mnemonic: EFFICacy = EFFECTive.

definition: shameless boldness; insolent audacity
examples: He had the effrontery to ask for a raise on his first day.
Her effrontery in interrupting the king shocked the whole court.
cloze: The thief had the {{effrontery}} to return and complain about the quality of the stolen goods.
mnemonic: EFFRONTERY: a FRONT of brass; a brazen face.

definition: believing that all people are equal and deserve equal rights
examples: The founders hoped to create an egalitarian society free of inherited privilege.
His egalitarian views led him to pay all employees an equal share.
cloze: The commune was strictly {{egalitarian}}; every member had equal rights and a vote.
mnemonic: EGALITARIAN: EQUAL (French égal).

definition: outstandingly bad; shockingly obvious
examples: Charging customers twice for the same order was an egregious error that angered everyone who noticed it.
The report listed egregious violations of safety rules, each one obvious and shocking to the inspectors.
cloze: The editor found an {{egregious}} mistake in the headline and had to reprint the whole issue.
mnemonic: E-GREGIOUS: stands out of the GREX (flock) like a black sheep, in a bad way.

definition: involving many careful details; complicated
examples: The ancient builders constructed an elaborate system of canals to carry water to the fields.
Peacocks perform elaborate displays of colorful feathers to attract mates during the breeding season.
cloze: The museum has an {{elaborate}} model of the city as it appeared in the Middle Ages.
mnemonic: E-LABOR-ate: made with LABOR.

definition: a mournful poem or song, especially for the dead
examples: The poet wrote an elegy for her friend who had died young.
The orchestra played an elegy in memory of the victims.
cloze: His poem was an {{elegy}}, mourning the loss of his village to the sea.
mnemonic: ELEGY: ELLie's GONE; a song for the dead.

definition: to draw out a response or reaction
examples: The comedian's joke elicited roars of laughter from an audience that had been sitting in stony silence.
Careful, gentle questioning finally elicited the full truth from the frightened witness, who had been silent for hours.

mnemonic: E-LICIT: bring out (e-) by luring (lacere).

definition: to completely remove or get rid of
examples: Vaccination programs have nearly eliminated smallpox from the world after decades of global effort.
Engineers redesigned the engine to eliminate unnecessary noise and vibration inside the passenger cabin.
cloze: Farmers hoped to {{eliminate}} the insects that were destroying their harvests.
mnemonic: E-LIMIT-ate: cut beyond the limit, remove.

definition: fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing
examples: The senator gave an eloquent speech, fluent and moving, that held the entire room spellbound for an hour.
Her eloquent and well-argued defense persuaded even the most skeptical members of the jury to reconsider.

mnemonic: ELOQUENT: speaks OUT (e-) with LOQUENT (speech) ease, like a smooth talker.

definition: to make clear; to explain
examples: The teacher used simple diagrams to elucidate the complex theory, so that even beginners could finally follow it.
Could you elucidate your reasoning for choosing this method over the cheaper alternative the others proposed?
cloze: The professor drew a chart to {{elucidate}} how the mechanism works.
mnemonic: E-LUCID-ate: make LUCID, clear as light.

definition: hard to find, catch, or define
examples: The elusive leopard, shy and nearly invisible in the forest, is rarely seen by tourists on safari.
Success remained elusive for the young company despite their best efforts, long hours, and several clever ideas.
cloze: The answer proved {{elusive}}, slipping away each time scientists thought they had found it.
mnemonic: ELUSIVE: ELUDES you.

definition: to come out or come into view; to become known
examples: A new theory emerged from the experiments carried out in the 1920s.
Insects emerge from the soil after heavy rains in early summer.
cloze: As the fog lifted, the shape of the mountain began to {{emerge}} in the distance.
mnemonic: E-MERGE: the opposite of submerge.

definition: famous and respected in a field
examples: The eminent surgeon, famous across the country for her skill, was invited to speak at the conference.

cloze: An {{eminent}} historian, she was consulted by presidents and professors alike.

definition: soothing, especially to the skin or to feelings
examples: She applied an emollient cream to her dry, cracked hands, and the soothing relief was almost immediate.
His emollient words, gentle and calming, soothed the angry crowd and prevented a fight from breaking out.
cloze: The diplomat's {{emollient}} tone softened the harsh criticisms that came before.
mnemonic: EMOLLIENT: MELT or soften, like a lotion.

definition: to give special importance or attention to something
examples: The professor emphasized the need to cite sources in every research paper.
Doctors emphasize the benefits of regular exercise for long-term health.
cloze: The report seeks to {{emphasize}} the role of education in reducing poverty.
mnemonic: EMPHASIZE: put the PHASE (focus) on it.

definition: based on observation or experiment rather than theory
examples: The theory needs empirical evidence before scientists will accept it.
She collected empirical data by measuring plant growth every day.
cloze: The study provides {{empirical}} proof, gathered from hundreds of experiments.
mnemonic: EMPIRICAL: EXPERIMENT and look.

definition: to imitate in an effort to equal or surpass
examples: Young musicians often try to emulate the great artists they admire, copying their style and practice habits.
She worked hard to emulate her mentor's calm, patient leadership style when she became head of the department.
cloze: Many students try to {{emulate}} the discipline of their favorite athletes.
mnemonic: EMULATE ~ EQUAL: you imitate a star hoping to EQUAL them.

definition: to meet or come across, often unexpectedly
examples: Explorers encountered fierce storms on their voyage across the Atlantic.
Researchers encountered several unexpected problems while collecting samples in the Arctic.
cloze: Students may {{encounter}} unfamiliar vocabulary in academic reading passages.
mnemonic: EN-COUNTER: come COUNTER to someone.

definition: regularly found in a particular place or group
examples: Malaria is endemic in many tropical regions, where the disease has existed for centuries among the local people.
Corruption was endemic in the old regime, so that almost every official accepted bribes as a normal practice.
cloze: Poverty is {{endemic}} in the region, affecting families generation after generation.
mnemonic: EN-DEMIC: within the DEMOS (people), always there.

definition: to weaken or drain of energy
examples: The tropical heat enervated the hikers, who could barely walk.
A long illness had enervated him, leaving him pale and listless.
cloze: The sweltering afternoon began to {{enervate}} even the strongest athletes.
mnemonic: E-NERVE-ate: takes the NERVE out of you. Not 'energize'!

definition: to cause or give rise to
examples: Poverty and hopelessness often engender crime and unrest, as people grow desperate for any way to survive.
The coach's fairness and honesty engendered deep trust among the players, who respected him for years afterward.
cloze: Rumors and secrecy tend to {{engender}} suspicion within an organization.
mnemonic: EN-GENDER: GENerate, give birth to.

definition: to improve the quality, value, or strength of something
examples: Good lighting can enhance the beauty of the artwork on display.
Farmers use fertilizers to enhance soil fertility and increase crop yields.
cloze: Regular practice will {{enhance}} your reading speed and comprehension.
mnemonic: EN-HANCE: add HEIGHT, raise the level.

definition: a puzzling person or thing
examples: The disappearance of the ship without a trace remains an enigma to historians, with no convincing explanation yet found.
To his friends, the quiet billionaire was an enigma, and nobody could say what he really wanted from life.
cloze: The artist's motives remain an {{enigma}}, since she never explained her paintings.
mnemonic: ENIGMA, the code machine that confused everybody.

definition: mysterious and difficult to understand

mnemonic: ENIGMA + tic: full of ENIGMA.

definition: deep, lasting hostility

cloze: Their {{enmity}} lasted for decades, passed from one generation to the next.

definition: listless boredom and dissatisfaction

The wealthy heirs suffered from ennui, having nothing to strive for and no goals worth pursuing.
cloze: A feeling of {{ennui}} settled over the town in the long, empty winter.
mnemonic: ENNUI sounds like 'on we...': a yawning sigh of boredom in French.

definition: very large in size, quantity, or extent

An enormous amount of data was collected during the five-year survey.
cloze: The volcano released an {{enormous}} cloud of ash high into the atmosphere.
mnemonic: E-NORM-ous: way beyond the NORM.

definition: to make certain that something happens
examples: Careful testing ensures that the new medicine is safe for patients.
Scientists use control groups to ensure that their results are reliable.
cloze: The government introduced laws to {{ensure}} clean air for all citizens.
mnemonic: EN-SURE: make SURE.

definition: the natural world, or the surroundings in which something exists
examples: Plastic waste causes serious harm to the marine environment and to the animals living there.
Children learn faster in an environment that encourages curiosity and welcomes their questions.
cloze: Plants must adapt to their {{environment}} in order to survive.
mnemonic: ENVIRON = surround: all that surrounds you.

definition: lasting for a very short time
examples: Fame can be ephemeral, vanishing as quickly as it arrived.
The ephemeral beauty of cherry blossoms draws crowds each spring.
cloze: Bubbles are {{ephemeral}}; they pop within seconds of forming.
mnemonic: EPHEMERAL: an EPHEMERAL mayfly lives one day.

definition: a perfect example or embodiment of something
examples: She is the epitome of grace and good manners, and everyone who meets her says the same.
The skyscraper, with its elegant glass walls, was the epitome of modern engineering and bold architectural design.
cloze: He was the {{epitome}} of generosity, giving away most of his fortune.
mnemonic: EPITOME: pronounced 'ee-PIT-uh-mee'; the PEAK of a thing.

definition: calmness and composure, especially under stress

The captain's steady equanimity calmed the nervous crew during the storm, so that nobody panicked.
cloze: Even under harsh criticism, he kept his {{equanimity}} and answered politely.
mnemonic: EQUAL + ANIM (mind): an equal, level mind.

definition: a state of balance between opposing forces
examples: The ecosystem remained in equilibrium until a new predator was introduced.
In economics, prices reach equilibrium when the quantity supplied exactly equals the quantity demanded.
cloze: The reaction slows as the system approaches {{equilibrium}}.
mnemonic: EQUI-LIBRIUM: EQUAL librium (libra scales).

definition: fair and impartial
examples: The court sought an equitable division of the property so that both heirs would feel treated fairly.
Teachers want an equitable system of grading that treats every student alike, regardless of family or background.
cloze: The two partners agreed on an {{equitable}} split of the profits.
mnemonic: EQUITABLE: EQUAL and fair.

definition: equal in value, amount, or meaning
examples: One inch of rain is roughly equivalent to ten inches of snow.
A degree from a foreign university is often considered equivalent to a local one.
cloze: The energy released was {{equivalent}} to that of several thousand tons of explosives.
mnemonic: EQUI-VALENT: equal value.

definition: open to more than one interpretation; deliberately ambiguous
examples: The test results were equivocal, so doctors ordered further tests.
His equivocal reply left us unsure whether he would accept the offer.
cloze: The senator gave an {{equivocal}} answer that could be read as either yes or no.
mnemonic: EQUI-VOCAL: two equal voices say two things.

definition: to use vague language to avoid committing to a position
examples: The minister equivocated when asked whether taxes would rise, giving a long, vague answer that said nothing.
Asked directly about the scandal, the CEO equivocated for several minutes without ever saying yes or no.
cloze: Voters grew impatient when the candidate continued to {{equivocate}} on the issue.
mnemonic: EQUI-VOCATE: EQUAL VOICES, speaking both ways.

definition: to destroy completely; to wipe out
examples: Vaccination programs helped eradicate smallpox from the whole world, so that the disease no longer exists anywhere.
Farmers worked tirelessly to eradicate the weeds that choked their crops, pulling them out by the roots.
cloze: Health officials hope to {{eradicate}} the disease entirely within a decade.
mnemonic: E-RADICATE: pull out by the ROOT (radix).

definition: to wear away gradually by wind, water, or other forces
examples: Rivers erode the rock over thousands of years, creating deep canyons.
Constant criticism slowly eroded the public's confidence in the government's ability to manage the economy.
cloze: Heavy rains can {{erode}} the soil on hillsides where trees have been cut down.
mnemonic: ERODE = ROD gets worn away by rain.

definition: straying from the proper course; wandering
examples: An errant golf ball, hit far off course, smashed the neighbor's window with a loud crash.
The errant knight traveled the country alone, wandering from village to village in search of adventure.
cloze: The {{errant}} child wandered away from the group and had to be found by the guide.
mnemonic: ERR-ant: ERRs from the path.

definition: unpredictable; lacking consistency
examples: His erratic behavior worried his friends, who never knew what strange thing he would do next.
The pilot reported erratic readings from the instruments, which jumped wildly up and down for no clear reason.
cloze: The patient's {{erratic}} heartbeat alarmed the doctors, who could not predict its changes.
mnemonic: ERRATIC: ERRs in direction, wanders (Latin errare).

definition: fake and inferior, used as a substitute
examples: During the war, people drank ersatz coffee made from roasted acorns.
The restaurant served an ersatz version of the classic dish.
cloze: The store sold {{ersatz}} leather made of plastic that cracked within weeks.
mnemonic: ERSATZ: a German word meaning 'replacement'.

definition: having or showing great learning
examples: The erudite professor could quote long passages from ancient texts from memory, in several languages.
Her erudite essays assumed that readers had studied history, philosophy, and literature for many years.
cloze: The library was filled with books for {{erudite}} scholars of medieval literature.
mnemonic: E-RUDE-ite: brought OUT of RUDE (rough, unlearned) state; polished by learning.

definition: to deliberately avoid or abstain from
examples: He eschews alcohol and caffeine completely, preferring to drink only water for the sake of his health.
Monks often eschew worldly pleasures and possessions so that they can concentrate fully on prayer and study.
cloze: The senator chose to {{eschew}} personal attacks and focus on policy.
mnemonic: ESCHEW sounds like 'ESCAPE-chew': you escape from it.

definition: understood by only a small group of specialists
examples: The lecture on esoteric branches of mathematics lost most of the audience.
He collects esoteric books that few people have ever heard of.
cloze: The club's {{esoteric}} rituals were known only to its members.
mnemonic: ESOTERIC: kept inside (Greek eso) a secret circle of insiders.

definition: to adopt or support a cause or belief
examples: The senator espoused the cause of tax reform for many years, speaking in its favor at every opportunity.
She espoused the idea of free education for all, and spent her whole career working to achieve it.
cloze: Many young activists {{espouse}} the cause of environmental protection.
mnemonic: ESPOUSE: you 'marry' (SPOUSE) a cause.

definition: absolutely necessary; fundamental
examples: Sunlight is essential for the growth of almost all green plants.
Reading widely is an essential habit for anyone preparing for university study.
cloze: Clean water is {{essential}} for human health and for agriculture.
mnemonic: ESSENTIAL: the ESSENCE, what the thing cannot lack.

definition: to set up on a firm basis; to prove something
examples: The first university in the region was established in the twelfth century.
The experiment helped establish a clear link between diet and heart disease.
cloze: Settlers worked together to {{establish}} a village beside the river.
mnemonic: ESTABLISH = STABLE base.

definition: to roughly calculate the size, value, or amount of something
examples: Scientists estimate that the glacier is about ten thousand years old.
Archaeologists estimated the city's population at around fifty thousand people.
cloze: It is difficult to {{estimate}} how many species of insects remain undiscovered.
mnemonic: ESTIMATE: EST. on a sign means roughly, not exact.

definition: relating to principles of right and wrong
examples: Scientists must follow strict ethical guidelines when conducting experiments on animals.
The article raised ethical concerns about collecting personal data without consent.
cloze: Doctors face difficult {{ethical}} decisions when resources are limited.
mnemonic: ETHICAL: ETHICS class teaches right and wrong.

definition: a speech or writing of high praise, especially for someone who has died
examples: His son delivered a moving eulogy at the funeral, praising his father's kindness, humor, and generosity.
The newspaper published a glowing eulogy for the late mayor, listing everything he had done for the town.
cloze: At the funeral, she delivered a {{eulogy}} full of warm memories of her grandfather.
mnemonic: EU (good) + LOGOS (word): good words.

definition: a mild word used in place of a harsh or blunt one
examples: 'Passed away' is a common euphemism for 'died', chosen because it sounds gentler and less blunt.
The company's euphemism 'downsizing' hid the unpleasant fact that hundreds of loyal workers were being fired.
cloze: The politician used a {{euphemism}}, calling the war 'a security operation' to make it sound milder.
mnemonic: EU (good) + PHEME (speech): speaking nicely.

definition: to judge the value or quality of something carefully
examples: Teachers evaluate students' essays on the basis of clarity and evidence.
Engineers evaluated several designs before choosing one for the new bridge.
cloze: The committee will {{evaluate}} each proposal and select the most promising project.
mnemonic: E-VALUE-ate: find the VALUE.

definition: quickly fading or disappearing
examples: The evanescent mist hung over the field at dawn but vanished completely as soon as the sun rose.
Their evanescent joy lasted only a moment and ended with the first news of the defeat.
cloze: The rainbow was {{evanescent}}, fading from the sky within minutes.
mnemonic: EVANESCENT: it VANISHES.

definition: after a long time or a series of events; in the end
examples: Over millions of years, the rock was eventually worn down into fine sand.
The scientists eventually discovered the cause of the mysterious illness.
cloze: The glacier will {{eventually}} disappear if global temperatures keep rising.
mnemonic: EVENT-ually: the final event.

definition: facts or signs that show whether something is true
examples: Fossils provide strong evidence that the continents were once joined together.
The detective gathered evidence before accusing anyone of the theft.
cloze: There is little {{evidence}} that the ancient city was ever attacked.
mnemonic: E-VIDENCE: you can VIEW the proof.

definition: clearly seen or understood; obvious
examples: It was evident from the fossil record that the climate had changed dramatically.
The effects of the drought were evident in the dry riverbeds and failed crops.
cloze: Her enthusiasm for the subject was {{evident}} in every lecture she gave.
mnemonic: E-VIDENT: you can VIDEo see it.

definition: to show clearly; to reveal a quality
examples: Her broad smile evinced her delight at the news, which she did not even try to hide.
The report evinces a deep understanding of the problem, showing that its authors studied it carefully for years.
cloze: His careful notes {{evince}} a mind with great attention to detail.
mnemonic: E-VINCE: conquer (vincere) the doubt by proving.

definition: to call up a feeling or memory
examples: The smell of baking bread evoked memories of her grandmother's kitchen.
The photograph evoked strong emotions in everyone who saw it.
cloze: Old songs can {{evoke}} vivid memories of childhood summers.
mnemonic: E-VOKE: call out (vox, voice).

definition: to develop gradually over time
examples: Birds evolved from small feathered dinosaurs over millions of years.
Language evolves constantly as new words are invented and old ones fall out of use.
cloze: Species must {{evolve}} new features to survive in changing environments.
mnemonic: E-VOLVE: roll (volv) out slowly.

definition: to make a problem or bad situation worse
examples: Scratching the rash will only exacerbate the irritation, making it redder, itchier, and more painful than before.
The new tax exacerbated the town's financial troubles, pushing several local shops to the edge of bankruptcy.
cloze: Pouring water on a grease fire will {{exacerbate}} the danger, not reduce it.
mnemonic: EX-ACERBATE: ACERB (sour) gets even more bitter.

definition: to dig out carefully, especially to uncover remains
examples: Archaeologists excavated the ruins of an ancient city buried under volcanic ash.
Workers excavated a deep trench before laying the pipes beneath the street.
cloze: The team plans to {{excavate}} the burial site next summer.
mnemonic: EX-CAVATE: take out of the CAVE/cavity.

definition: to go beyond a limit or be greater than something
examples: Annual rainfall in the region can exceed three meters during the monsoon season.
The results exceeded the researchers' expectations by a wide margin.
cloze: The number of visitors began to {{exceed}} the capacity of the national park.
mnemonic: EX-CEED: go out (ex) beyond the limit.

definition: to keep out or leave out of consideration
examples: The study excluded participants who had a history of heart disease.
Historians have often excluded women's stories from accounts of the past.
cloze: Researchers must {{exclude}} other possible causes before they can identify the true source.
mnemonic: EX-CLUDE: shut (clude) out.

definition: to clear from blame or guilt
