definition: to throw overboard or discard something unneeded or burdensome
examples: The crew had to jettison cargo to keep the sinking boat afloat.
After the merger, the company decided to jettison several unprofitable product lines.
cloze: To lighten the overloaded balloon, the pilot chose to {{jettison}} the sandbags and rise above the storm.
mnemonic: JET-tison: a jet dumps fuel to lighten its load.

definition: extreme, aggressive patriotism, especially favoring warlike foreign policy
examples: The newspaper's jingoism pushed readers to demand war over a minor border dispute.
Critics condemned the senator's jingoism as reckless flag-waving that ignored the cost of conflict.
cloze: The rally's {{jingoism}} alarmed diplomats, who feared the crowd's belligerent nationalism would provoke a war.
mnemonic: JINGO sounds like 'by jingo!' — a loud patriot itching for a fight.

definition: fond of joking; humorous and playful
examples: The jocular host kept the whole dinner table laughing with his silly stories.
Despite the tense meeting, her jocular tone made everyone relax and smile.
cloze: Normally serious, the professor was in a {{jocular}} mood and teased students with puns throughout the lecture.
mnemonic: JOKEr — a jocular person jokes.

definition: showing good judgment and sound sense
examples: Her judicious use of limited funds kept the small charity running through the recession.
A judicious editor trims only what weakens the story and leaves the rest alone.
cloze: The manager made a {{judicious}} decision, weighing every risk carefully before approving the expensive purchase.
mnemonic: JUDGE-icious: a good judge shows good judgment.

definition: to show or prove that something is reasonable
examples: Scientists must justify their conclusions with reliable evidence.
The high cost of the telescope was justified by the discoveries it made.
cloze: The author tried to {{justify}} her decision to omit the final chapter.
mnemonic: JUST (fair) + IFY: make it fair.

definition: to place side by side to compare or contrast
examples: The museum chose to juxtapose ancient pottery with modern ceramics to show how styles evolved.
The film juxtaposes scenes of lavish parties with images of poverty outside the gates.
cloze: The artist likes to {{juxtapose}} bright, cheerful colors with grim subject matter for a jarring effect.
mnemonic: JUXTA means 'next to' — put things next to each other.

definition: praise and honor received for an achievement
examples: The entire team received kudos from the director for finishing the project ahead of schedule.
She earned kudos from critics for her bold and thoughtful first novel.
cloze: The chef received {{kudos}} from diners and reviewers alike for the restaurant's inventive new menu.
mnemonic: KUDOS sounds like 'good-os' — good things said about you.

definition: complicated and confusing like a maze
examples: Tourists quickly got lost in the narrow, labyrinthine alleys of the ancient walled city.
The labyrinthine tax code baffled even experienced accountants who had studied it for years.
cloze: Applicants struggled through the {{labyrinthine}} bureaucracy, passing from office to office without any answers.
mnemonic: Labyrinth: the Minotaur's maze in Crete.

definition: using very few words; terse
examples: The laconic cowboy answered every question with a single word or a shrug.
Her laconic reply, just 'No', ended the debate faster than any speech could.
cloze: Known for his {{laconic}} style, the general replied to the long accusation with a single curt sentence.
mnemonic: Laconia (Sparta): Spartans were famous for brief, blunt speech.

definition: to criticize harshly
examples: Reviewers lambasted the new film as a bloated, incoherent mess that wasted both money and talent.
The coach lambasted his players in the locker room after the humiliating defeat.
cloze: Newspapers continued to {{lambaste}} the mayor for ignoring the flooding crisis in poorer districts.
mnemonic: LAMB-BASTE: imagine basting (beating) a poor lamb with words.

definition: to mock or ridicule publicly, usually through satire
examples: The comedy show lampooned the president's awkward speeches in sketches that aired week after week.
Cartoonists have long lampooned politicians by exaggerating their features and mocking their habits in print.
cloze: The magazine would {{lampoon}} anyone in power with sharp satirical sketches and cartoons.
mnemonic: LAMPoon: shine a LAMP on foolishness and tease it.

definition: lacking energy; slow and relaxed, often pleasantly
examples: On the hot afternoon, the languid cat stretched out and refused to move.
She gave a languid wave from the hammock, too relaxed to say hello.
cloze: The {{languid}} pace of the island, where nobody hurried, soothed the stressed tourists.
mnemonic: LANGUish — to languish is to droop without energy.

definition: generous giving of money or gifts; the gifts themselves
examples: The university depended on the largess of wealthy alumni to fund its new library.
The king distributed largess to the poor on his coronation day.
cloze: Thanks to the donor's {{largess}}, the struggling school finally received new computers and books.
mnemonic: LARGE-ss: a large gift.

definition: a state of physical or mental weariness; lack of energy
examples: A deep lassitude settled over the town during the long, humid summer afternoons.
After the marathon, he felt a heavy lassitude and could barely climb the stairs.
cloze: The sudden {{lassitude}} that overcame the patient was a warning sign that the illness was returning.
mnemonic: LASS-itude: LASt of your energy is gone.

definition: present but hidden or not yet active
examples: The virus can remain latent in the body for years before symptoms appear.
Her latent talent for music emerged only when she picked up a guitar at thirty.
cloze: Teachers sought to uncover the {{latent}} abilities of students who had never been given a chance to shine.
mnemonic: LATENT sounds like 'late' — shows up late, hiding till then.

definition: to praise highly
examples: Critics lauded the young pianist for her flawless and emotional performance.
The mayor lauded the volunteers whose tireless work saved the town's library.
cloze: The committee chose to {{laud}} the scientist publicly for her groundbreaking discovery.
mnemonic: LAUD sounds like 'loud' — praise out LOUD.

definition: deserving praise, even if not fully successful
examples: Her laudable effort to feed the homeless earned the town's respect.
The team's goal was laudable, even though the project ultimately fell short.
cloze: Cutting waste to protect the environment is a {{laudable}} aim that most people would applaud.
mnemonic: LAUD + ABLE: able to be praised.

definition: extravagant, given or spent in great quantity
examples: The billionaire threw a lavish party with fireworks, live orchestras, and gourmet food.
They showered the new baby with lavish gifts far beyond what was needed.
cloze: Despite the firm's losses, the executives continued their {{lavish}} lifestyle of private jets and luxury hotels.
mnemonic: LAVish — LAVa flowing freely, a flood of excess.

definition: not strict, careful, or severe
examples: Lax airport security allowed a dangerous item to slip unnoticed through the checkpoint last month.
Her lax approach to deadlines frustrated the entire team and delayed the whole project.
cloze: Because the landlord was {{lax}} about enforcing the rules, tenants regularly ignored them.
mnemonic: LAX sounds like 'relax' — too relaxed about rules.

definition: allowed by law or reasonable and valid
examples: The rebels did not recognize the legitimate government of the province.
Historians raised legitimate questions about the reliability of the chronicle.
cloze: Only a {{legitimate}} claim to the land would be accepted by the court.
mnemonic: LEGIT: LEGal and fair.

definition: sluggish, lacking energy or enthusiasm
examples: The heat left the whole class feeling lethargic and unable to concentrate.
After the huge meal, he felt lethargic and wanted only to nap on the couch.
cloze: The patient was pale and {{lethargic}}, barely able to raise his head from the pillow.
mnemonic: LETHE, river of forgetfulness: so sleepy you forget to move.

definition: humor or lack of seriousness, especially at an inappropriate time
examples: A moment of levity relieved the tension in the long, grim negotiation.
The judge scolded the lawyer for treating the serious charges with levity.
cloze: His joke brought a brief note of {{levity}} to an otherwise solemn funeral service.
mnemonic: LEVIty = LIGHT (like 'elevate'); opposite of GRAVITY.

definition: morally unrestrained, especially in sexual matters
examples: The novel scandalized readers with its portrayal of a licentious aristocracy.
Puritan leaders condemned the theater as a school of licentious behavior.
cloze: The poet's {{licentious}} lifestyle, filled with wild parties and affairs, shocked polite society.
mnemonic: LICENSE to do anything — a licentious person has no limits.

definition: in the same way; also
examples: Frogs breathe partly through their skin; salamanders likewise absorb oxygen this way.
The first group received a lecture; the second group was likewise given printed notes.
cloze: Some birds migrate thousands of miles each year, and many butterflies {{likewise}} travel great distances.
mnemonic: LIKE + WISE: in a like manner.

definition: to treat as a celebrity; to give great attention and praise to
examples: The press lionized the astronauts and invited them to every important event.
After the victory, the city lionized its young captain as a national hero.
cloze: Society tends to {{lionize}} athletes while giving little recognition to teachers and nurses.
mnemonic: Treat someone like a LION — king of beasts.

definition: lacking energy or interest
examples: The listless students stared out the window, uninterested in the lesson.
After weeks of illness, she felt listless and showed no appetite or enthusiasm.
cloze: The team gave a {{listless}} performance, moving slowly and showing no sign of ambition.
mnemonic: Without a LIST of goals, you're LISTLESS.

definition: reluctant, unwilling
examples: She was loath to leave her hometown, where all her friends lived.
Experts are loath to predict the outcome while evidence remains so limited.
cloze: The senator was {{loath}} to criticize his party's leader, fearing the consequences.
mnemonic: LOATHe means hate; loath (no e) = hating to do something.

definition: to find the position of something
examples: Archaeologists used radar to locate the buried foundations of the temple.
The company decided to locate its new factory near the river.
cloze: Sonar helps scientists {{locate}} shipwrecks on the ocean floor.
mnemonic: LOCATE = LOCATION: find the place.

definition: very talkative
examples: The loquacious taxi driver chatted about politics, weather, and football for the entire ride.
Shy at first, she became loquacious once the topic turned to her favorite novels.
cloze: Our {{loquacious}} neighbor can turn a quick hello into an hour-long conversation.
mnemonic: LOQU- means speak: a LOQUacious person LOQs (talks) a lot.

definition: clear and easy to understand; also rational and clear-minded
examples: The teacher's lucid explanation made the difficult theorem suddenly easy to follow.
Though very ill, the old man remained lucid and recalled every detail of the event.
cloze: The author's prose is so {{lucid}} that even complex economic ideas become simple to grasp.
mnemonic: LUCId contains LUX/light: light makes things clear.

definition: producing a great deal of profit
examples: He left teaching for a lucrative career in investment banking.
The company signed a lucrative contract that doubled its annual revenue.
cloze: Selling rare coins turned out to be a surprisingly {{lucrative}} hobby that earned him a fortune.
mnemonic: LUCRe sounds like LUCRative: filthy lucre means money.

definition: looking or sounding sad and dismal, often exaggeratedly
examples: The lugubrious violin music made the already gloomy funeral feel even heavier.
He wore a lugubrious expression all week, as though the whole world had let him down.
cloze: The dog's {{lugubrious}} howl echoed through the empty house, a mournful sound that chilled everyone.
mnemonic: LUGUBrious: a LUG-ging, BRIO-less (lifeless) mood.

definition: to soothe or calm, often into a false sense of security
examples: Soft music and the gentle rocking of the cradle lulled the baby to sleep within minutes.
Years of peace lulled the city into believing that an attack could never happen.
cloze: The con artist's friendly manner was meant to {{lull}} victims into trusting him with their savings.
mnemonic: A LULLaby lulls you to sleep.

definition: giving off light; bright; also brilliantly clear
examples: The luminous moon lit the path through the dark forest.
Critics praised the luminous prose of the memoir, so clear it seemed to glow.
cloze: The deep-sea fish had a {{luminous}} lure that glowed in the lightless water to attract prey.
mnemonic: LUMINary, ILLUMINate: all about light.

definition: shocking, sensational; or glaringly vivid in color
examples: Tabloids filled their front pages with lurid details of the scandal.
The sunset turned the sky a lurid orange that seemed almost unnatural.
cloze: The author was criticized for the {{lurid}} descriptions of violence that seemed designed only to shock readers.
mnemonic: LURID — 'lure' of horrid details that lure readers.

definition: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful
examples: The magnanimous winner praised her opponent and offered to help him train.
He was magnanimous in victory, refusing to gloat over the defeated team.
cloze: Instead of seeking revenge, the king was {{magnanimous}} and pardoned the rebels who had surrendered.
mnemonic: MAGNA (great) + ANIMUS (soul): a great soul.

definition: a wealthy and influential person, especially in business
examples: The shipping magnate owned dozens of tankers and a famous football club.
As a media magnate, he controlled newspapers, radio stations, and television channels across the country.
cloze: The steel {{magnate}} used his vast fortune to shape the nation's politics for decades.
mnemonic: MAGNate: has MAGNitude of wealth.

definition: to keep something in good condition or continue it
examples: Volunteers maintain the trails so hikers can cross the mountains safely.
Mammals maintain a constant body temperature regardless of the weather outside.
cloze: The museum must {{maintain}} a stable temperature to protect its fragile manuscripts.
mnemonic: MAIN-TAIN: hold with the MAIN hand.

definition: clumsy or awkward; lacking skill or tact
examples: The maladroit waiter dropped a tray of glasses in front of the guests.
His maladroit handling of the delicate negotiation left both sides offended.
cloze: Her {{maladroit}} remark about the host's cooking embarrassed everyone at the table.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + ADROIT (skilled): badly skilled.

definition: having or showing a wish to do evil
examples: The villain gave the hero a malevolent smile before locking the door.
She felt a malevolent presence watching her from the dark corner.
cloze: The {{malevolent}} rumor was spread by a rival who wanted nothing but to ruin the senator's reputation.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + VOLENT (wishing): wishing bad.

definition: to speak harmful untruths about; slander
examples: Rivals tried to malign her reputation by spreading false rumors about her past work.
He felt unjustly maligned by newspapers that portrayed him as a crook.
cloze: Politicians frequently {{malign}} their opponents with accusations that have no basis in fact.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + sign — speaking bad.

definition: easily shaped or influenced
examples: Gold is highly malleable and can be hammered into extremely thin sheets.
Young children's malleable minds absorb languages far more easily than adults'.
cloze: The politician's opinions proved {{malleable}}, changing whichever way the powerful donors pushed them.
mnemonic: MALLET: you can hammer it into shape.

definition: the edge or border; an amount of difference
examples: The candidate won by a narrow margin of only two votes.
Monks wrote notes in the margins of the ancient manuscript.
cloze: Small businesses often have a very low profit {{margin}} in their first few years.
mnemonic: MARGIN: the MARGIN of a page is the edge.

definition: fully grown or developed
examples: Mature trees in the old forest can reach heights of seventy meters.
The economy of the region became mature once heavy industry was established.
cloze: Salmon return to the river where they hatched once they become {{mature}}.
mnemonic: MATURE: MATure by the time you are grown.

definition: tearfully and foolishly sentimental
examples: After three drinks he became maudlin, weeping over old memories of his schooldays.
Critics dismissed the film as a maudlin melodrama designed to force tears.
cloze: The speaker's {{maudlin}} tribute, full of exaggerated sobbing, embarrassed the guests more than it moved them.
mnemonic: Mary MAGDALENE is often painted weeping — 'maudlin' evolved from her name.

definition: an independent person who refuses to follow the group or conform
examples: The maverick scientist ignored the consensus and pursued her own unpopular theory.
A political maverick, he often voted against his own party.
cloze: As a {{maverick}} in the fashion world, she rejected trends and designed clothes in her own odd style.
mnemonic: Named for Samuel Maverick, whose cattle roamed unbranded.

definition: sentimental in a feeble or sickly way
examples: The mawkish love song was so sugary and sentimental that it made even romantic listeners cringe.
Critics dismissed the novel's ending as mawkish and manipulative, a shameless attempt to draw tears.
cloze: The greeting card's {{mawkish}} verse was so syrupy that it made her laugh instead of cry.
mnemonic: MAWKish: a MAWful sticky-sweet taste.

definition: to wander aimlessly; or to follow a winding course
examples: The river meanders through the valley before reaching the sea.
On Sundays they would meander through the market without any plan.
cloze: The speaker tended to {{meander}} from topic to topic, never really reaching his main point.
mnemonic: Maeander River in Turkey famously winds back and forth.

definition: a system of parts or a process that produces an effect
examples: The study describes the mechanism by which plants absorb water.
Scientists discovered a defense mechanism that allows the frog to survive freezing.
cloze: The clock's {{mechanism}} consists of hundreds of tiny gears working together.
mnemonic: MECHANISM: MECHANical works.

definition: lying; dishonest
examples: The mendacious witness was exposed when his story contradicted the video evidence.
Voters grew tired of the mendacious claims in the candidate's advertisements.
cloze: The {{mendacious}} salesman made false promises about the car's history to close the deal.
mnemonic: MEN-DACIOUS: 'men deceive us.'

definition: motivated chiefly by money
examples: Critics accused the agent of mercenary motives rather than genuine concern for his clients.
The mercenary soldier fought for whichever army paid the most.
cloze: Her {{mercenary}} attitude was obvious: she would only help if the pay was high enough.
mnemonic: MERCenary — MERCantile: all about money.

definition: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood
examples: Her mercurial temper meant staff never knew whether she would praise or scold them.
The mercurial star was adored one week and booed the next.
cloze: The {{mercurial}} dictator would be charming at breakfast and furiously cruel by lunch.
mnemonic: Mercury (quicksilver) moves fast and changes shape.

definition: showing great attention to detail; very careful
examples: The meticulous accountant checked every figure twice before signing the report.
Her meticulous notes allowed the team to reconstruct the experiment exactly.
cloze: A {{meticulous}} restorer spent months repairing the painting, correcting every tiny crack with patience.
mnemonic: METICulous: a METIC-ulous person measures every detail like a meter.

definition: to move from one region or habitat to another
examples: Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometers to warmer forests each autumn.
Many rural workers migrated to cities during the industrial revolution.
cloze: Several species of whales {{migrate}} to tropical waters to breed during winter.
mnemonic: MIGRATE: MIGhty trip, GRATE-ful to arrive.

definition: a person who hates or distrusts other people
examples: The misanthrope lived alone on a mountain, avoiding all human contact.
Molière's famous play portrays a misanthrope disgusted by the hypocrisy of society.
cloze: A confirmed {{misanthrope}}, he declined every invitation and complained about the stupidity of humanity.
mnemonic: MIS (hate) + ANTHROPOS (man); opposite of PHILANTHROPE.

definition: a wrong or inaccurate name or term
examples: Calling the small hill a mountain is a misnomer, since it is barely two hundred feet high.
'Peanut' is a misnomer because the peanut is actually a legume rather than a nut.
cloze: It is a {{misnomer}} to call the whale a fish, because whales are mammals.
mnemonic: MIS (wrong) + NOM (name): wrong name.

definition: to make less severe or harmful
examples: Planting trees can mitigate the effects of urban heat during summer.
The judge reduced the sentence because of mitigating circumstances in the defendant's past.
cloze: Engineers added extra drainage to {{mitigate}} the risk of flooding after heavy rains.
mnemonic: MITigate sounds like 'mitt': a mitt softens a blow.

definition: a small amount of something
examples: He showed not even a modicum of remorse for what he had done.
With a modicum of effort, you could have passed the test.
cloze: The scheme succeeded only because the victims had a {{modicum}} of trust and little time to verify it.
mnemonic: MODEst amount — a MODicum is a small measure.

definition: to change something slightly, usually to improve it
examples: Engineers modified the bridge design after the first tests revealed weaknesses.
Farmers have modified crops over centuries through selective breeding.
cloze: The author had to {{modify}} several chapters to satisfy the editor's concerns.
mnemonic: MODIFY = MODe-ify: change the mode.

definition: to soothe the anger of; to appease
examples: The airline offered free tickets to mollify the angry passengers.
Nothing she said could mollify her furious boss after the missed deadline.
cloze: The manager tried to {{mollify}} the irate customer with a refund and a sincere apology.
mnemonic: MOLLify: make MOLLusk-soft; soften anger.

definition: to pamper or overprotect
examples: Parents who mollycoddle their children may prevent them from learning independence.
The coach refused to mollycoddle the players and made them run extra laps.
cloze: Critics say that the school tends to {{mollycoddle}} students instead of preparing them for real challenges.
mnemonic: A MOLLY (girl) COD-dled like a delicate egg.

definition: gloomy, sullen, and withdrawn
examples: He sat morose and silent at the party, refusing to join any conversation.
The long winter left the villagers feeling morose and irritable.
cloze: After losing his job, he became {{morose}}, staying in his room and speaking to nobody.
mnemonic: MOROSE sounds like 'more sore' — more sad and grumpy.

definition: having many varied parts or kinds
examples: The city's multifarious culture includes cuisines and customs from every continent.
A manager must handle the multifarious demands of staff, clients, and budgets.
cloze: The curator's {{multifarious}} collection ranged from ancient coins to modern robots.
mnemonic: MULTI (many) + 'variety' — many varieties.

definition: ordinary, dull, everyday
examples: After the excitement of travel, she returned to the mundane routine of office life.
He wrote about mundane events, like making breakfast, with surprising beauty.
cloze: Despite her glamorous image, her daily life was filled with {{mundane}} chores such as laundry and shopping.
mnemonic: MUNDANE comes from 'mundus' (world): worldly, everyday.

definition: very generous
examples: The munificent donor gave millions to build the new hospital wing.
Guests were overwhelmed by the munificent hospitality of their hosts.
cloze: Thanks to the {{munificent}} gift of a local philanthropist, the library was able to double its collection.
mnemonic: MUNI (gifts) + FICENT (make): one who makes gifts.

definition: liable to change
examples: Public opinion is mutable and can shift dramatically within a single week.
Early scientists believed the species were fixed, but later evidence showed they are mutable.
cloze: Fashion is a {{mutable}} thing, constantly shifting from one season to the next.
mnemonic: MUTate: able to mutate.

definition: countless; extremely numerous
examples: The night sky displayed myriad stars far from any city lights.
Immigrants face myriad challenges, from language barriers to unfamiliar customs.
cloze: The ocean hosts a {{myriad}} of creatures, from tiny plankton to enormous whales.
mnemonic: MYRIAD = ten thousand in Greek; too many to count.

definition: the lowest point
examples: The company hit its nadir when profits collapsed and half the staff were laid off.
For the team, the humiliating defeat was the nadir of the season.
cloze: His career reached its {{nadir}} when he lost his job, his home, and his savings in a single year.
mnemonic: NADIR sounds like 'down'; opposite of ZENITH.

definition: just coming into existence; beginning to develop
examples: The nascent democracy faced many challenges in building its institutions.
Investors were wary of the nascent technology, which was still unproven.
cloze: The {{nascent}} movement began as a small group of students but soon grew across the country.
mnemonic: NASCENT ~ NATAL: just born.

definition: vague, unclear, lacking definite form
examples: The manager gave only a nebulous plan, leaving the staff confused about what to do.
His nebulous ideas about the future never turned into a real strategy.
cloze: The contract's {{nebulous}} wording left both sides unsure of what was actually required.
mnemonic: A NEBULA is a hazy cloud.

definition: wicked or criminal
examples: Detectives uncovered the villain's nefarious plot to steal the city's gold reserves.
The company's nefarious practices included bribing officials and hiding toxic waste.
cloze: The {{nefarious}} scheme to defraud pensioners was uncovered by an investigative journalist.
mnemonic: NE (not) + FAS (right): not right.

definition: a beginner; a person new to a subject or activity
examples: The neophyte skier fell repeatedly on her first day on the slopes.
As a neophyte in politics, he had much to learn about compromise.
cloze: Experts patiently guide each {{neophyte}} who joins the club and has never held a camera before.
mnemonic: NEO (new) + PHYTE (plant): a new plant.

definition: not supporting either side; having no strong features
examples: Switzerland stayed neutral during both world wars.
Scientists should remain neutral when presenting data to the public.
cloze: The mediator took a {{neutral}} position and did not favor either party in the dispute.
mnemonic: NEUTRAL: NEITHER side.

definition: calm and casually unconcerned
examples: He remained nonchalant while everyone else panicked about the approaching storm.
She gave a nonchalant shrug, as though winning the prize meant nothing.
cloze: Despite the high stakes, the pilot was {{nonchalant}} about the turbulence and kept sipping his coffee.
mnemonic: NON + CHALANT (be warm): not warmed up about it.

definition: an unimportant person or thing
examples: Before the election, he was a political nonentity whom few voters could even name.
Ignored by the bosses, she felt like a nonentity in the large corporation.
cloze: The new clerk was treated as a {{nonentity}}, ignored by managers and rarely invited to meetings.
mnemonic: NON + ENTITY: not a being of importance.

definition: so surprised and confused that one is unsure how to react
examples: The sudden question left the speaker nonplussed, unable to say a word.
She was nonplussed by the stranger's odd gift and simply stared.
cloze: The candidate was {{nonplussed}} by the unexpected accusation and stood speechless at the podium.
mnemonic: NON + PLUS: no more (moves) to make.

definition: a standard or pattern regarded as typical
examples: Arranged marriage was the norm in many traditional societies.
Students who break academic norms can face serious penalties.
cloze: Rapid technological change has become the {{norm}} in modern industry.
mnemonic: NORM = NORMal.

definition: a questionable remedy or pet solution claimed to cure problems
examples: Politicians offered simple nostrums for the complex economic crisis, none of which actually worked.
He sold a bottle of colored water as a miracle nostrum for baldness.
cloze: The doctor refused to prescribe the so-called {{nostrum}}, a useless tonic marketed as a cure-all.
mnemonic: NOSTRUM = 'our' in Latin: 'our own secret' remedy.

definition: worthy of attention because of importance
examples: Darwin made notable observations during his voyage to the Galapagos Islands.
The region is notable for its ancient cave paintings.
cloze: One {{notable}} exception to the pattern is the platypus, which lays eggs.
mnemonic: NOTE-able: worth taking NOTE of.

definition: a belief, idea, or understanding of something
examples: The notion that the Earth was flat was rejected by ancient Greek scholars.
Students often hold the mistaken notion that memorizing is the same as understanding.
cloze: Early philosophers developed the {{notion}} that everything in nature is made of tiny particles.
mnemonic: NOTION: a NOTE in your mind.

definition: famous for something bad
examples: The notorious bandit had already escaped from three prisons and was wanted in several states.
The restaurant is notorious for its rude waiters, long delays, and consistently terrible service.
cloze: The street was {{notorious}} for pickpockets, so tourists were warned to avoid it at night.
mnemonic: NOTable for the wrong thing: NOTorious.

definition: a person new to a field or activity
examples: A novice at chess, she lost her first ten games.
The novice chef followed the recipe step by step, afraid to improvise.
cloze: Even a {{novice}} could use the simple software without any training.
mnemonic: NOVICE contains NOVel/NEW.

definition: harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant
examples: Factories released noxious fumes that made it hard for nearby residents to breathe.
A noxious smell drifted from the neglected pond and made everyone nearby cover their faces.
cloze: Workers were required to wear masks to avoid breathing the {{noxious}} gases released by the chemicals.
mnemonic: NOX = harm; NOXious = NOT OK for you.

definition: a subtle difference in meaning, expression, or tone
examples: A good translator captures every nuance of the original poem.
The debate lacked nuance, reducing a complex issue to slogans.
cloze: Only a native speaker could grasp the subtle {{nuance}} that separated the two similar words.
mnemonic: NU-ance = a tiny NEW shade (nuage = cloud in French).

definition: to make legally invalid; to cancel out
examples: The court's ruling nullified the contract because one party had been misled.
One careless decision can nullify months of careful work by the entire design team.
cloze: The new evidence could {{nullify}} the verdict and force the court to hold a fresh trial.
mnemonic: NULL means zero; nullify = make zero.

definition: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course
examples: The obdurate negotiator refused every compromise, no matter how reasonable.
Despite pleas from his family, the old man remained obdurate and would not sell the farm.
cloze: The {{obdurate}} dictator ignored all appeals from world leaders and refused to step down.
mnemonic: OB-DURATE: DURable like a hard rock; won't bend.

definition: deferential respect; a gesture of submission such as bowing
examples: The courtiers made deep obeisance to the queen as she entered the hall.
The tribe paid obeisance to the chief by kneeling before him.
cloze: Visitors were expected to show {{obeisance}} to the emperor by bowing low in his presence.
mnemonic: OBEY-sance: you obey and bow.

definition: to make unclear or hard to understand
examples: The company used technical jargon to obfuscate the true cost of the plan.
Lawyers often obfuscate the issue with legal language rather than clarify it.
cloze: Instead of answering honestly, the official tried to {{obfuscate}} the facts with confusing statistics.
mnemonic: OB (over) + FUSC (dark): cover with darkness.

definition: based on facts rather than personal feelings
examples: A good historian tries to give an objective account of events.
Scientists use objective measurements to avoid bias in their experiments.
cloze: The judge made an {{objective}} decision based solely on the evidence.
mnemonic: OBJECT-ive: look at the OBJECT, not your feelings.

definition: unaware of or not concerned about what is happening around one
examples: Wearing headphones, he was oblivious to the loud siren behind him.
She was oblivious to the stares as she hummed down the hallway.
cloze: The tourist, {{oblivious}} to the danger, wandered happily into the path of the oncoming cyclist.
mnemonic: OBLIVion — you forget everything around you.

definition: strong public condemnation; disgrace resulting from it
examples: The traitor died in obloquy, hated by the country he betrayed.
She endured years of obloquy from the press after the failed expedition.
cloze: The disgraced official lived out his days in {{obloquy}}, shunned by former friends and colleagues.
mnemonic: OB + LOQU (speak): speak against.

definition: not well known; hard to understand
examples: The little-known poet was obscure during her life, and only gained fame after her death.
The instructions were so obscure that no one could assemble the shelf.
cloze: Few people have heard of the author, a rather {{obscure}} figure in nineteenth-century literature.
mnemonic: OBSCURE: covered (ob) in dark (scur).

definition: excessively eager to please or obey; fawning
examples: The obsequious assistant laughed at every one of his boss's feeble jokes.
Waiters hovered around the celebrity in an obsequious manner, bowing and flattering.
cloze: The senator was surrounded by {{obsequious}} aides who agreed with everything he said.
mnemonic: OBSEQUIOUS ~ 'OB-SEQUel': follows behind you like a sequel.

definition: no longer used; out of date
examples: Typewriters quickly became obsolete once affordable personal computers arrived in most homes and offices.
The old software is obsolete and no longer receives updates.
cloze: Technology moves so quickly that last year's phone may already be {{obsolete}} today.
mnemonic: OBSOLETE: has 'slipped' out (soleo) of use.

definition: stubbornly refusing to change one's mind
examples: The obstinate child refused to eat anything except pasta, no matter what his parents offered.
Her obstinate refusal to listen to advice led to repeated mistakes.
cloze: The {{obstinate}} mule would not move, no matter how hard the farmer pulled the rope.
mnemonic: OBSTINATE — 'obstacle' in the path of your plans.

definition: to get or acquire something
examples: Researchers obtained soil samples from deep beneath the Antarctic ice.
Students must obtain permission from the library before borrowing rare books.
cloze: Biologists were able to {{obtain}} DNA from fossilized bones that were thousands of years old.
mnemonic: OB-TAIN: TAIN-t your hand holding it: you got it.

definition: slow to understand; insensitive or dull
examples: He was too obtuse to notice the hints that she wanted him to leave.
Her obtuse reply showed she had missed the point of the joke.
cloze: Are you being deliberately {{obtuse}}, or do you truly not see why the plan failed?
mnemonic: OBTUSE angle is blunt, not sharp; blunt mind.

definition: to remove a need or difficulty; to make unnecessary
examples: The new software obviates the need for employees to enter all the data manually.
Careful planning can obviate many problems before they arise and save the team considerable time.
cloze: A well-designed bridge would {{obviate}} the long detour that commuters now take each morning.
mnemonic: OBVIATE: get OUT of the VIA (way) — the obstacle is removed.

definition: to happen or take place
examples: Earthquakes occur most often along the edges of tectonic plates.
Mutations occur naturally in all living organisms.
cloze: Many accidents {{occur}} when drivers are tired and cannot focus on the road.
mnemonic: OCCUR: a thing that RUNS (curr) up to you.

definition: extremely unpleasant; deserving hatred
examples: The odious landlord raised rents on the poorest tenants every month.
Betraying a lifelong friend for money is an odious act that few people ever forgive.
cloze: Most people found the dictator's cruelty {{odious}} and called for the world to condemn him.
mnemonic: ODIous sounds like ODIOUS - you hate it, an ODD, ODOR.

definition: annoyingly eager to give orders or interfere
examples: The officious clerk insisted on checking every form three times, annoying the customers.
An officious neighbor kept offering unwanted advice about my garden.
cloze: Visitors found the {{officious}} guard irritating as he ordered them around over trivial rules.
mnemonic: OFFICIOUS: acts like he runs the OFFICE.

definition: to balance or cancel out the effect of something
examples: Higher exports offset the decline in domestic sales.
Planting trees can offset some of the carbon released by factories.
cloze: The company tried to {{offset}} rising costs by raising its prices slightly.
mnemonic: OFF + SET: set off against the loss.

definition: suggesting that something bad will happen
examples: Dark ominous clouds gathered above the picnic, warning of a coming storm.
The ominous silence from the enemy camp worried the soldiers.
cloze: An {{ominous}} rumble from the volcano told the villagers it was time to flee.
mnemonic: OMEN-ous: an omen of trouble.

definition: burdensome; requiring great effort
examples: The onerous task of auditing every account took the team months.
Small businesses complained about the onerous regulations that cost time and money.
cloze: Caring for three young children on her own was an {{onerous}} responsibility that left her exhausted.
mnemonic: ONERous contains ONUS: a burden.

definition: continuing to happen; still in progress
examples: Researchers have an ongoing study of the glacier's rate of melting.
The ongoing drought has damaged farms throughout the valley.
cloze: There is an {{ongoing}} debate among historians about the causes of the empire's decline.
mnemonic: ON + GOING: still going on.

definition: not transparent; hard to understand
examples: The window was made of opaque glass, so no one could see inside.
The scientist's opaque writing made the findings difficult for ordinary readers to follow.
cloze: Critics complained about the government's {{opaque}} decision-making, which hid its reasoning from the public.
mnemonic: OPAQUE ~ 'opacity': you can't see through it.

definition: harsh public criticism or disgrace
examples: The scandal brought public opprobrium upon the senator and his family.
Her decision to betray the team was met with widespread opprobrium.
cloze: The company faced international {{opprobrium}} after reports of its unsafe factories emerged.
mnemonic: O-PROB-rium: PROBlem for your reputation.

definition: ostentatiously rich and luxurious
examples: The opulent palace had golden staircases and crystal chandeliers in every hall.
Their opulent lifestyle included yachts, private chefs, and a dozen vacation homes.
cloze: Guests were stunned by the {{opulent}} ballroom, with its gilded ceilings and priceless tapestries.
mnemonic: OPULENT ~ 'opulence' ~ OPEN wallet.

definition: elaborately decorated
examples: The cathedral's ornate ceiling was covered in gold leaf and carved angels.
She wrote in an ornate style, full of long sentences and flowery phrases.
cloze: The king sat on an {{ornate}} throne decorated with jewels, carvings, and golden vines.
mnemonic: ORNAment — ORNATE means full of ornaments.

definition: bad-tempered and stubborn
examples: The ornery old farmer scowled at everyone who walked across his field.
The ornery mule refused to carry any load that morning.
cloze: Grandpa grows {{ornery}} whenever anyone tries to rearrange his tools or reorganize his shed.
mnemonic: ORNERY sounds like 'ordinary' gone sour.

definition: conforming to established or traditional beliefs
examples: The doctor rejected orthodox treatments in favor of experimental ones.
Her orthodox views on education matched the school's long-standing traditions.
cloze: The professor's ideas were hardly {{orthodox}}, often shocking colleagues who clung to the established theories.
mnemonic: ORTHO (right) + DOX (opinion): right opinion.

definition: to swing back and forth; to waver between choices
examples: The pendulum oscillated steadily back and forth, ticking away each second inside the old clock.
Voters oscillate between the two parties, never staying loyal for long.
cloze: The manager continued to {{oscillate}} between expansion and cost-cutting, unable to make a decision.
mnemonic: OSCILLATE ~ OSCILLoscope waves going up and down.

definition: appearing to be true, but not necessarily real
examples: The ostensible reason for the trip was business, though they spent the week at the beach.
His ostensible friendliness hid a deep desire to see his rival fail.
cloze: The {{ostensible}} purpose of the meeting was to share news, but the real goal was to remove the director.
mnemonic: OSTENSIBLE ~ ostentatious: 'on show', only for show.

definition: showy, designed to impress or attract attention
examples: Their ostentatious mansion, with golden gates and marble lions, annoyed the neighbors.
He avoided ostentatious displays of his wealth and drove an ordinary car.
cloze: The tycoon's {{ostentatious}} parties, complete with ice sculptures and diamond favors, were meant to impress.
mnemonic: OSTENT = show; ostentatious people put on a show.

definition: to exclude someone from a group by general consent
examples: Villagers ostracized the family after the scandal and refused to speak to them.
Teenagers who dress differently are sometimes ostracized by their classmates.
cloze: The club chose to {{ostracize}} the cheater, banning him from every game and gathering.
mnemonic: Ancient Greeks voted to banish with OSTRAKA (pottery shards).

definition: the result of an action or process
examples: The outcome of the election surprised even the experts.
Educators measure learning outcomes to see whether the program works.
cloze: The final {{outcome}} of the experiment depends on the temperature of the water.
mnemonic: OUT + COME: what comes out.

definition: to extend over and cover part of something
examples: The ranges of the two bird species overlap in the central valley.
The courses overlap, so students who take both will see some topics twice.
cloze: The roles of the two departments {{overlap}}, which causes confusion about who is responsible.
mnemonic: OVER + LAP: lay over each other.

definition: done or shown openly; not hidden
examples: There was no overt hostility between the rivals, though tension filled the room.
The party's overt support for the policy surprised no one.
cloze: His {{overt}} contempt for the rules was obvious to everyone, and he made no attempt to hide it.
mnemonic: OVERT ~ 'over' the table, in the open.

definition: to quiet or calm a troubled person
examples: The mother tried to pacify the crying baby by humming a gentle song and rocking the cradle.
Officials sought to pacify the angry protesters by promising a full investigation into the incident.
cloze: Only a sincere apology could {{pacify}} her furious client.
mnemonic: PACIFY: PACIFIC ocean = peaceful.

definition: to ease the severity of something without curing it
examples: Painkillers can palliate the symptoms, but they do not cure the disease.
The government tried to palliate public anger with small temporary measures.
cloze: The nurse used warm compresses to {{palliate}} the pain until the doctor arrived.
mnemonic: PALLIATE: a PAL helps you feel better.

definition: a supposed remedy that cures all problems
examples: No single policy is a panacea for the nation's economic troubles.
Some patients view the new drug as a panacea, though it treats only one condition.
cloze: Technology is often presented as a {{panacea}}, but it cannot solve every social problem.
mnemonic: PAN (all) + ACEA (cure): cures all.

definition: a typical model or pattern that shapes how a field thinks
examples: Darwin's theory of evolution became the dominant paradigm for understanding the diversity of living things.
The discovery forced physicists to abandon the old paradigm and build an entirely new framework.
cloze: Copernicus's work triggered a {{paradigm}} shift that changed how astronomers pictured the universe.
mnemonic: PARA + DIGM: a pair of dimes set the standard model.

definition: a person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a quality
examples: She was a paragon of diligence, never missing a deadline in twenty years.
The village held up the retired teacher as a paragon of integrity and kindness.
cloze: The new chancellor was hailed as a {{paragon}} of fairness, admired even by her rivals.
mnemonic: A PAIR of GONE flaws: nothing wrong — a perfect model.

definition: a limit or measurable factor that defines a system
examples: Scientists set the parameters of the experiment before collecting any data.
Temperature is a key parameter in determining the rate of the reaction.
cloze: The study operated within strict {{parameter}} to ensure the results could be compared.
mnemonic: PARA (beside) + METER: measure beside the rules.

definition: a person rejected and shunned by society
examples: After the scandal, he became a pariah in the city's business community.
The whistleblower was treated like a pariah by her former colleagues.
cloze: The regime's isolation turned the country into an international {{pariah}}, cut off from most trade.
mnemonic: PARIAH: sounds like 'Pariah = pah, a rejected one'.

definition: extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy
examples: The parsimonious landlord refused to repair the heater even in the coldest winter.
Her parsimonious habits meant she reused tea bags and wrapping paper for years.
cloze: Despite his vast fortune, the {{parsimonious}} old man haggled over every penny of the bill.
mnemonic: PARSI-MONEY-ous: he pars down every bit of money he spends.

definition: strongly supporting one side, often blindly and without balance
examples: The partisan crowd booed every decision the referee made against the home team.
Debate in the legislature grew so partisan that no compromise seemed possible.
cloze: The commission's report was criticized as {{partisan}} because it ignored all evidence favoring the opposition.
mnemonic: PARTISAN takes a PART — only one part, one side.

definition: a small or insufficient amount of something
examples: The paucity of rainfall left the reservoirs nearly empty by August.
Critics noted a paucity of original ideas in the otherwise polished film.
cloze: A {{paucity}} of reliable data made it impossible to draw firm conclusions from the study.
mnemonic: PAUCITY sounds like 'poor city' — poor in supplies.

definition: overly concerned with minor rules and displays of learning
examples: The pedantic editor corrected every comma but missed the article's larger flaws.
His pedantic lectures on grammar bored students who simply wanted to communicate clearly.
cloze: She grew tired of her {{pedantic}} colleague, who interrupted meetings to correct trivial errors in pronunciation.
mnemonic: PEDANT = 'ped' like pedal: he pedals on tiny details endlessly.

definition: lacking inspiration; dull
examples: The film's pedestrian script offered no surprises, and the audience could predict every scene in advance.
His pedestrian prose bored readers who had hoped for something original, lively, or at least memorable.
cloze: The meal was {{pedestrian}}, neither bad nor memorable.
mnemonic: PEDESTRIAN: walking on foot — slow plodding.

definition: transparently clear, in appearance or in style
examples: The pellucid mountain stream allowed us to see every pebble on the bottom.
Her pellucid prose made even the most complex economic theory easy to follow.
cloze: The lawyer's {{pellucid}} explanation left the jury with no doubt about the sequence of events.
mnemonic: PELLUCID contains LUCID, meaning clear.

definition: a strong and continuing liking or inclination for something
examples: He has a penchant for old jazz records and spends weekends searching used shops.
The young chef's penchant for bold spices made her dishes unforgettable.
cloze: Her {{penchant}} for risky investments eventually cost the family most of its savings.
mnemonic: PENCHANT: a PEN CHANT — she loves to chant while writing with a pen.

definition: feeling sorrow for having done wrong
examples: The penitent thief returned the stolen jewels to their owner and tearfully asked for forgiveness.
He stood penitent before the judge, hoping that his sincere remorse would earn him a lighter sentence.
cloze: The {{penitent}} sinner knelt and begged for forgiveness.
mnemonic: PENITENT: PENANCE — you do penance when sorry.

definition: extremely poor; or very stingy
examples: The penurious student lived on bread and tea for most of the winter.
He was penurious even in his later wealth, refusing to turn on the lights.
cloze: After the factory closed, the once-thriving town became {{penurious}}, with families struggling to buy food.
mnemonic: PENURY sounds like 'pen-you-ry': you have only a pen, no money.

definition: to become aware of something through the senses or mind
examples: Bees perceive ultraviolet light that humans cannot see.
Many consumers perceive handmade goods as higher in quality.
cloze: Infants can {{perceive}} differences between sounds long before they can speak.
mnemonic: PER + CEIVE: take in through the senses.

definition: lasting for a very long time; constantly recurring
examples: Traffic jams are a perennial problem in the capital, appearing every single morning and evening without fail.
The garden's perennial flowers return each spring without any need for the owner to replant them.
cloze: Flooding is a {{perennial}} concern for villages along the river, which recur nearly every spring.
mnemonic: PER + ANNUAL: through the years.

definition: deceitful and untrustworthy; disloyal
examples: The perfidious general secretly sold the army's plans to the enemy.
She felt betrayed by her perfidious friend, who had spread rumors behind her back.
cloze: History remembers him as a {{perfidious}} ally who broke every treaty the moment it became inconvenient.
mnemonic: PERFIDIOUS: 'per-FIDO-us' — a dog (Fido) that is NOT faithful.

definition: deliberate betrayal of trust
examples: History remembers the general mainly for his perfidy, since he sold secrets to the enemy during the war.
The peace treaty collapsed because of the perfidy of its signers, who had never intended to honor it.
cloze: The spy's {{perfidy}} cost many soldiers their lives.
mnemonic: PERFIDY: no FIDELITY.

definition: done routinely with little interest or care
examples: He gave the report only a perfunctory glance before signing it.
The clerk's perfunctory apology did little to calm the angry customer.
cloze: The inspector's {{perfunctory}} check missed the cracks that later caused the bridge to close.
mnemonic: PERFUNCTORY: 'per-FUNCTION' — just going through the function.

definition: of secondary importance; located at the edge
examples: The mayor's role in the project was merely peripheral, and he attended almost none of the meetings.
Peripheral vision lets you notice movement at the very edge of your field of sight.
cloze: These details are {{peripheral}} to the main argument and can safely be left out.
mnemonic: PERIPHERAL: PERIMETER — the outer edge.

definition: causing harm in a gradual, subtle way
examples: Rumors can have a pernicious effect on a team's morale over time.
Scientists warned of the pernicious influence of pollutants that build up slowly in the soil.
cloze: The {{pernicious}} spread of misinformation slowly eroded the public's trust in the health system.
mnemonic: PERNICIOUS: sounds like 'pernicious = perish-ious' — it makes things perish.

definition: to confuse someone completely
examples: The strange noise coming from the engine continued to perplex even the most experienced engineers in the shop.
Her sudden silence at the meeting perplexed everyone at the table, since she normally had plenty to say.
cloze: The complicated instructions continued to {{perplex}} even the most experienced users.
mnemonic: PERPLEX: PER + PLEX (tangled): tangled thoughts.

definition: to continue firmly despite difficulty
examples: Symptoms of the disease persisted for several weeks.
Some ancient customs persist in remote villages even today.
cloze: If the drought continues to {{persist}}, farmers will be forced to abandon the land.
mnemonic: PERSIST = PERSevere + exIST.

definition: a particular way of viewing things
examples: Historians offer a new perspective on the causes of the war.
Studying abroad gave her a broader perspective on world cultures.
cloze: From a biological {{perspective}}, the behavior helps the species survive.
mnemonic: PER + SPECT: look through to see.

definition: having keen insight; mentally sharp in understanding
examples: The perspicacious detective noticed the single detail everyone else had overlooked.
A perspicacious investor, she sensed the market's collapse months before it happened.
cloze: Her {{perspicacious}} reading of the negotiations helped her predict the rival's next move.
mnemonic: PERSPICACIOUS: you can see (spic = look) right through things.

definition: spreading widely through every part of something
examples: A pervasive smell of smoke filled the entire building after the fire.
Social media has become a pervasive part of teenage life.
cloze: The {{pervasive}} sense of fear in the city kept people off the streets after dark.
mnemonic: PERVASIVE: it PERVADES — goes everywhere, like a pervading smell.

definition: childishly sulky or bad-tempered
examples: The petulant child threw his toys when told to go to bed.
Her petulant reply showed that she was still angry about losing.
cloze: The star's {{petulant}} refusal to leave his dressing room delayed the show for an hour.
mnemonic: PETULANT: like a PET that is spoiled and whines.

definition: an observable fact or event, especially a remarkable one
examples: The northern lights are a natural phenomenon caused by charged solar particles.
Urbanization is a global phenomenon that has reshaped modern society.
cloze: Scientists are still trying to explain the strange {{phenomenon}} of ball lightning.
mnemonic: PHENOMENON: PHEN-omenal event you can see.

definition: calm and not easily excited or upset
examples: The phlegmatic pilot kept his voice steady even as the engine sputtered.
Her phlegmatic temperament made her an ideal negotiator in tense situations.
cloze: Unlike his excitable brother, he remained {{phlegmatic}} when the results arrived, simply nodding and returning to work.
mnemonic: PHLEGM makes you sluggish — a phlegmatic person is slow to react.

definition: to arouse curiosity or interest
examples: The mysterious letter without a return address piqued her curiosity, and she opened it at once.
The documentary piqued many students' interest in astronomy, and several later joined the school's science club.
cloze: The strange symbol on the door was enough to {{pique}} the visitors' curiosity.
mnemonic: PIQUE: a PEEK at a pique of curiosity.

definition: concise and forcefully meaningful in expression
examples: His pithy remarks summed up the entire debate in a single sentence.
Proverbs are pithy sayings that carry a lot of wisdom in few words.
cloze: The editor praised the writer's {{pithy}} style, in which every sentence carried real weight.
mnemonic: PITHY: the PITH is the core of an orange — the essence.

definition: of crucial importance because other things depend on it
examples: The pivotal moment of the game came in the final minute, when the goalkeeper saved a penalty.
She played a pivotal role in the negotiations, bringing both sides together after weeks of deadlock.
cloze: The court's ruling proved {{pivotal}} to the outcome of the election.
mnemonic: PIVOTAL: a PIVOT — the point that everything turns on.

definition: to calm someone's anger by giving in or making concessions
examples: The manager offered a refund to placate the furious customer.
Nothing the mayor said could placate the crowd demanding his resignation.
cloze: The company tried to {{placate}} angry shareholders by promising higher dividends next year.
mnemonic: PLACATE sounds like 'PLACID' — make someone placid.

definition: a dull, overused remark presented as if it were fresh
examples: The speech was full of platitudes about hard work and never giving up.
Offering a platitude like 'everything happens for a reason' comforted no one.
cloze: Rather than offering real solutions, the senator hid behind a {{platitude}} about the importance of family values.
mnemonic: PLATITUDE: a flat PLATE of attitude — flat, dull words.

definition: seeming reasonable and believable
examples: The detective found his alibi plausible but could not verify it with any witnesses.
It is plausible that prices will rise again next year, given the current shortage of supplies.
cloze: Her {{plausible}} excuse for being late convinced the teacher.
mnemonic: PLAUSIBLE: APPLAUSE-ible: worth applause because it makes sense.

definition: an excessive or very large amount of something
examples: The menu offered a plethora of choices, which left every one of us unable to decide.
A plethora of evidence pointed to the defendant's guilt, and the jury convicted him quickly.
cloze: Shoppers faced a {{plethora}} of brands, each claiming to be the healthiest choice.
mnemonic: PLETHORA: 'plenty-ora' — plenty!

definition: evoking a keen sense of sadness or sympathy
examples: The film's poignant ending, in which the old friends said goodbye, left many viewers in tears.
He gave a poignant speech about the childhood friends he had lost over the years.
cloze: The soldier's last letter home was a {{poignant}} reminder of the war's human cost.
mnemonic: POIGNANT: sounds like 'point' — it pierces the heart.

definition: a strong written or spoken attack on a belief or policy
examples: The columnist's polemic against the new tax outraged many readers.
Her book is less a balanced study than a fierce polemic against industrial farming.
cloze: The pamphlet was a bitter {{polemic}} aimed at everyone who had supported the war.
mnemonic: POLEMIC: sounds like 'poll-EMIC' — arguing about politics, not a calm poll.

definition: slow and clumsy because of great weight; dull and labored
examples: The ponderous elephant lumbered slowly and heavily across the dusty clearing toward the watering hole.
His ponderous prose made the annual report a long and tiresome chore to read.
cloze: The professor's {{ponderous}} lecture, heavy with jargon, put half the class to sleep.
mnemonic: PONDEROUS: pound-erous — heavy as a pound.

definition: to speak in a pompous, dogmatic way
examples: He loved to pontificate about politics at family dinners, ignoring everyone who tried to disagree with him.
The critic pontificated for an hour on what real art should be and who could be called an artist.
cloze: Rather than listen, the professor would {{pontificate}} to students on every subject.
mnemonic: PONTIFF (pope) pontificates — speaks as an authority.

definition: a sign that something important or bad is about to happen
examples: Dark clouds on the horizon were a portent of the coming storm.
Many saw the sudden loss of power as a portent of worse trouble.
cloze: The falling bird numbers were a {{portent}} of ecological trouble to come.
mnemonic: PORTENT: a PORT-ent — a ship in port warns of a storm.

definition: possible but not yet realized
examples: Researchers warned of the potential dangers of the new chemical.
The company sees great potential customers among university students.
cloze: Geologists identified several {{potential}} sites for the new mine.
mnemonic: POTENTIAL: POTent in the future.

definition: dealing with problems in a practical rather than idealistic way
examples: Her pragmatic approach focused on what would actually work rather than what sounded noble.
The pragmatic mayor chose a cheaper repair over an ambitious but unaffordable rebuild.
cloze: Rather than chase an ideal solution, the {{pragmatic}} committee settled on a plan it could actually afford.
mnemonic: PRAGMATIC: 'pragma' means deed in Greek — focus on deeds that work.

definition: to talk foolishly or at length about trivial things
examples: The children prattled happily about toys and cartoons through the entire long car ride to the coast.
He prattled on about the weather for an hour, never noticing that nobody was listening.
cloze: Guests continued to {{prattle}} about celebrity gossip all evening.
mnemonic: PRATTLE: sounds like 'rattle' of talking.

definition: dangerously unstable or uncertain
examples: The climber's precarious position on the narrow ledge made everyone nervous.
With sales falling, the small firm's financial situation became increasingly precarious.
cloze: He lived a {{precarious}} existence, never sure whether he could pay next month's rent.
mnemonic: PRECARIOUS: sounds like 'pre-carry-us' — about to drop us.

definition: to come before something in time or order
examples: A series of small tremors often precedes a major earthquake.
In most textbooks, a summary precedes the detailed chapters.
cloze: The invention of the written alphabet had to {{precede}} the development of widespread literacy.
mnemonic: PRE (before) + CEDE (go): go before.

definition: done suddenly and without careful thought
examples: Selling the house so quickly was a precipitate decision that he would later come to regret.
The government's precipitate withdrawal from the region left the local population in chaos and confusion.
cloze: Critics accused the president of a {{precipitate}} decision that was made before the facts were known.
mnemonic: PRECIPITATE: rain 'precipitates' from the sky suddenly — falls headlong.

definition: to make something impossible; to prevent in advance
examples: A knee injury precluded him from playing in the final.
The contract's wording precludes either party from ending the deal early.
cloze: Her tight schedule will {{preclude}} any chance of a vacation before the end of the year.
mnemonic: PRE + CLUDE (close): close the door before it opens.

definition: a person or thing that comes before and leads to another
examples: The telegraph was an early precursor of the modern telephone, paving the way for later inventions.
Economic uncertainty is often a precursor to political unrest, as history has shown many times.
cloze: The small experiment proved to be a {{precursor}} to a major scientific breakthrough.
mnemonic: PRE + CURSOR: the one that runs before.

definition: to say what will happen in the future
examples: Meteorologists use satellite data to predict the path of hurricanes.
Economists struggled to predict the collapse of the housing market.
cloze: Scientists cannot yet {{predict}} exactly when a volcano will erupt.
mnemonic: PRE (before) + DICT (say): say before.

definition: a strong preference or special liking for something
examples: He has a predilection for spicy food that surprises his guests.
Her predilection for mystery novels filled the shelves of her small apartment.
cloze: The director's {{predilection}} for dark, moody settings is evident in all his films.
mnemonic: PRE-DIL-ection: you 'pre-elect' what you like.

definition: most common or most powerful among several
examples: Wheat was the predominant crop in the region throughout the nineteenth century.
The predominant view among economists changed after the financial crisis.
cloze: In this ecosystem, grasses are the {{predominant}} form of plant life.
mnemonic: PRE-DOMINANT: DOMINANT already.

definition: coming before the main part; preparatory
examples: Preliminary results suggest that the new drug may reduce inflammation.
The committee held a preliminary meeting to set the agenda for the conference.

definition: a statement that proves an argument false

mnemonic: REBUTTAL: RE + BUT: she says 'but'.

mnemonic: RECTITUDE: RECT = right, straight.

examples: The refractory mule would not move an inch, no matter how hard the farmer pulled and pleaded.

cloze: The {{refractory}} patient refused all treatment, despite the doctor's repeated pleas.

definition: to make someone or something look or feel young again

cloze: A good night's sleep can {{rejuvenate}} even the most tired traveler.

definition: to assign to a lower or less important position
examples: After the mistake, he was relegated to a desk in the basement.
The team was relegated to the second division after a poor season.
cloze: The new manager tried to {{relegate}} her rivals to minor roles in the project.
mnemonic: RELEGATE: RE + LEGATE: send back to a lower rank.

definition: able to be trusted to be consistent and correct
examples: Radar is a reliable tool for tracking storms.
Historians need reliable sources to reconstruct the past.

mnemonic: RELY + ABLE: you can rely on it.

definition: to voluntarily let go of something

cloze: The general was forced to {{relinquish}} command after the defeat.

definition: unwillingness or hesitation to do something

mnemonic: RELUCTANT + ce: noun of hesitance.

definition: unwilling and hesitant to do something

definition: an expression of disapproval or disappointment

definition: to reject as untrue or unjust; to disown
